# Born of a virgin — Isaiah 7:14, Genesis 3:15, Micah 5:2–3

*This page is generated from [`arguments/TestimonyArguments/BornOfAVirgin`](https://github.com/testimonyproject/testimony/blob/main/arguments/TestimonyArguments/BornOfAVirgin). Every heading and paragraph below is a docstring in those files; every formula is rendered from the encoding they check. If the page and the source disagree, the page is the one that is wrong, and regenerating it is the fix.*

Atoms are numbered propositional variables, numbered once for the whole page, so the same variable means the same claim in every position below. [Reading the logic](../reading-the-logic.md) is the short version of what the notation means. A result marked ⚗ is one this library constructs rather than reports.

## TestimonyArguments.BornOfAVirgin — Isaiah 7:14, Genesis 3:15, Micah 5:2–3

Matthew 1:22–23 quotes Isaiah 7:14 as grounds that the Messiah is born of a
virgin. Unlike Micah 5:2 (see `BornInBethlehem`), the predictive reading here is
heavily disputed, and the dispute is lexical: both sides grant that the Hebrew
עַלְמָה (*almah*) denotes a young woman of marriageable age, and they dispute
whether it denotes a virgin; the Septuagint's παρθένος is read as "virgin" —
though whether it meant that in the translator's own day is disputed too
(`Dispute.Septuagint`). Isaiah's immediate context — a
sign to Ahaz, apparently fulfilled within the prophet's own generation (cf. Isa
8:3–4) — is read by most critical and much Jewish scholarship as having nothing
to do with a future Messiah.

The argument now runs on **four scriptural strands**, and that changes its
shape. Each is encoded as a `Line` — its own grounds, its own inference step,
what it delivers — and the packages are assembled from those rather than from
flat premise lists. `Lines.lean` is where the shape of the argument is legible
in one screen.

**The Isaianic strand** is the one above, hinging on *almah*.

**The protoevangelium strand** reads Genesis 3:15 — enmity between the serpent's
seed and "her seed", זֶרַע הָאִשָּׁה — as the first promise of a redeemer, and
takes the matrilineal wording to mark a birth with no human father, since
Hebrew ordinarily reckons זֶרַע through the man. That last step is genuinely
contestable and is marked `disputed`. Some readers who grant the messianic
reading deny it, the Lutheran commentators Leupold and Keil among them. Leupold
allows that the wording refers to the virgin birth "Not primarily, but at least
incidentally", and holds that "the expression used does not specifically
prophesy the virgin birth, but it coincides and agrees with it under divine
providence". Others affirm it:
Luther and Henry. And Genesis itself speaks of a woman's seed in ordinary
births, of Hagar's (16:10) and of Rebekah's (24:60). `Results.Genesis` and
`Dispute.Genesis` weigh it (below).

**The Michean strand** reads Micah 5:2–3 — "until the time when she who is in
labour has given birth" — as naming a mother and no father for the coming
ruler. The objection is immediate and is encoded as the rival: this is an
argument from silence, and an oracle about a woman in labour has no occasion to
mention a father.

**The referential strand answers the lexical dispute without entering it.**
`almah` need not *mean* "virgin" for Mary to *be* an `almah`. Genesis settles
the compatibility outright: Rebekah is an עַלְמָה at 24:43 and a בְּתוּלָה "whom no
man had known" at 24:16, the same woman under both terms. Mary was a betrothed
young woman of marriageable age and conceived as a virgin, so she answers
Isaiah's description on anyone's lexicon — and `semantic_establishes` shows
that Matthew's claim therefore never required the sense the objection demands.

That reply has a price, and `compatibility_does_not_establish_criterion` names
it: the argument is purely defensive. It defeats the objection without
delivering the criterion, which still has to come from one of the four
scriptural strands. What it buys is that *losing* the lexical dispute no longer
costs the fulfilment claim.

**The versional evidence is encoded in full, including the half that tells
against the reading.** Targum Jonathan renders עוּלֵימְתָא, "young woman", and does
not read 7:14 messianically though it reads 9:5–6 and 11:1 so; Aquila,
Symmachus and Theodotion render νεᾶνις. Against them, the pre-Christian
Septuagint renders παρθένος — "virgin", on Rico and Gentry's reading of its
Greek, though not on Wegner's (below) — and the Syriac Peshitta ܒܬܘܠܬܐ,
"virgin", its only ܒܬܘܠܬܐ for עַלְמָה. So the Aramaic evidence is itself split:
the Targum against the Peshitta, whose translator may have been a Jewish
Christian who knew the Greek (van der Kooij), and whose 7:14 may follow the
Septuagint (Chen). 1QIsaᵃ, copied before Christ, reads עַלְמָה as the Masoretic
Text does. The verse has other variants, but none at the word, so no textual
variant rescues either side: the dispute is about the word's sense, not its
text. The usual Christian reply, that the Three revised
against Christian use, is now one party's ground: Rico and Gentry's case from
usage leans on it, and Davidson and Meade read the revision the other way
(`Dispute.Septuagint`). Whether Theodotion's version is itself pre-Christian,
which would give the revision a reason with no polemic in it, the library has
not yet found a source to cite, and it is left out of the reckoning.

`compatibility_defeats_lexical_objection` is where the tension pays off.
Granting every versional datum and adding the referential premises, the
objection no longer reaches its conclusion — because once virginity is
compatible with the word, four translators making four different choices about
how much of the referent to make explicit is not evidence about the sense.

**The Septuagint's own witness is weighed in full, and it does less than it is
usually asked to.** The argument is Irenaeus's: Jews translated Isaiah into
Greek "much before the period of our Lord's advent", so their παρθένος cannot be
a Christian reading put on the text (*Against Heresies* III.21.1).
`septuagintWitness_establishes` grants it everything it needs and checks that it
goes through. Three results then say what it rests on and what it reaches.

- **It rests on one word** (`parthenos_is_load_bearing`). Without the claim that
  παρθένος, in the translator's Greek, means a virgin, the Septuagint shows
  nothing about the woman. Rico and Gentry hold that it does, "whenever it
  appears in Semitic Koine Greek", and Bratcher agrees. Wegner, Rhodea and Meade
  deny it, and point to Genesis 34:3, where the Greek calls Dinah a παρθένος
  after Shechem has lain with her; Walton doubts it, from classical usage.
  The Greek Pentateuch, the corpus that verse comes from, uses the word in its
  laws where virginity is the point (Leviticus 21:13–14, Deuteronomy
  22:13–21), and its law of the seduced παρθένος reads Wegner's verse otherwise:
  the woman a man has lain with is still the law's παρθένος, owed "the
  bride-price of virgins" (Exodus 22:15–16), and Genesis 34 tells Shechem's act
  in that law's words. `Dispute.Septuagint` weighs the five, and **the
  Septuagint's side prevails** (`septuagint_prevails_over_wegner`): the status
  reading of Genesis 34:3 defeats Wegner, and he, resting on a step rated
  `disputed`, is too weak to answer it. The claims about the word exclude each
  other by what they mean — Wegner's says the word meant a young woman and not
  yet a virgin — and the dispute is computed with that. The verdict turns on one
  rating, the status reading's step, `plausible` because no reader found grants
  its grounds and denies it, and no higher because no reader found makes it.
  Were it `disputed`, nothing would prevail; `Dispute.Septuagint` says so, with
  where the evidence on each side lies.
- **Scripture's own reading of the word turns on the standard**
  (`matthew_step_turns_on_the_standard`). Matthew quotes the Septuagint's ἡ
  παρθένος of Mary, who conceived before she and Joseph came together, so in
  the text he quotes the word means "virgin". Wegner grants what Matthew says
  and holds that the word had changed in meaning since the translator wrote it.
  Under the evidence standard that is a credible critique, and Matthew and
  Wegner stand off. Under the Scripture standard — Scripture interprets
  Scripture, so a dissent from a step grounded in Scripture alone must rest on
  Scripture too — Wegner's argument from early Greek usage is not heard, and
  Matthew's reading prevails. `Dispute.Matthew` reports both.
- **It shows how one early reader read Isaiah, not what Isaiah's word means**
  (`septuagint_word_rests_on_its_inference`). Granted its sense, the Septuagint
  shows that a Jewish translator before Christ read the woman of 7:14 as a
  virgin — so that reading is no Christian invention. The step from his Greek to
  Isaiah's Hebrew is a further one, and rated `disputed`: Irenaeus takes it,
  holding the Greek inspired; Bratcher, Brown and Walton deny it. On Bratcher's
  and Brown's reading a rendering can follow the woman described rather than the
  word: the translator of Genesis wrote παρθένος for the עַלְמָה Rebekah (24:43),
  whom the story has already called a virgin, and elsewhere the Septuagint's
  translators render עַלְמָה with νεᾶνις four times. That is also the referential
  strand's reading of the versions.
- **It leaves the conception open** (`septuagint_leaves_the_conception_open`).
  The Greek says the virgin *shall* be with child. A woman who is a virgin when
  the sign is given and later conceives in the ordinary way fits it; so does a
  virgin who conceives as a virgin, as Justin reads it. The first is not only a
  rival's reading: Bratcher, who holds that παρθένος "definitely means 'virgin'
  in the LXX", calls it "the most reasonable explanation" of the Greek of 7:14.
  So even granted the word, the Septuagint does not decide, and the virginal
  conception comes, if it comes, from the promise of a sign (`signLine`) or from
  Matthew and Luke.

**"Her seed" is weighed as the Septuagint's word is, and it too does less than
it is often asked to.** Genesis 3:15 names the seed as the woman's, and the
strand's hinge reads that as marking a birth with no human father.
`Results.Genesis` reads "marks" both ways (`whatHerSeedMarks`).

- **As what the wording itself signifies**, it is Luther's argument: the seed of
  other women "might rather be said to have been the seed of the man", but
  Mary's was "the true Seed of Mary". He finds the sense in the words of
  Genesis, and holds that Isaiah later "threw some additional light" on it. It
  rests on his step (`her_seed_rests_on_its_inference`). The Lutheran
  commentators Leupold and Keil, who hold the virgin birth, grant every ground
  and deny it; so does Jack P. Lewis (*Journal of the Evangelical Theological
  Society*, 1991), who doubts the promise reading itself but argues without
  needing that doubt. Weighed
  against Leupold and Lewis, **nothing prevails**
  (`nothing_prevails_over_her_seed`): Luther's reading can be defended, and so
  can theirs. But the tie is nearer to breaking against Luther than for him. One
  rating would break it against him: Lewis's step, `disputed` only on the
  Catholic apologist Jimmy Akin, who grants Lewis's point about the idiom and
  still calls the wording "odd", agreeing with the "many" who have "rightly
  seen" it as "a hint of the Virgin Birth". Two would be needed to break it for
  him: his own step, and the claim that Genesis 3:15 is the protoevangelium at
  all, which critical readers deny.
- **As what the wording fits, once fulfilled**, it is granted by Leupold and
  Keil. Leupold: "it coincides and agrees with it under divine providence".
  But they reach the fit from the conception, so read this way the verse
  confirms the virgin birth to one who already believes it, and gives no reason
  to believe it to one who does not.
- **The promise is fulfilled in Jesus, and the fulfilment confirms it**
  (`Dispute.Protoevangelium`). Every term of the verse is met as the New
  Testament names it: the woman's seed in the Son "made of a woman" (Galatians
  4:4); the serpent in "that old serpent, called the Devil" (Revelation 12:9);
  its head crushed when the Son destroys the devil "through death" (Hebrews
  2:14; 1 John 3:8); his heel struck in his death, and the wound not the end of
  him (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Irenaeus, Calvin, Keil, Leupold and Hamilton read
  it so. The fulfilment confirms that the verse was a promise, by a rated step
  and not by deduction, and it does so without the virgin birth
  (`the_confirmation_does_not_need_the_virgin_birth`). With the virginal
  conception it says one thing more: the seed in whom the promise is fulfilled
  was of the woman alone (`seed_of_the_woman_alone`). That does not show the
  wording foretold it (`the_fulfilment_does_not_reach_the_wording`). Weighed
  against Westermann, who denies that the verse is any promise, from the
  collective "seed" and the form of a punishment oracle, **nothing prevails**
  (`nothing_prevails_over_the_promise`): the fulfilment's step is `disputed` on
  him, and his on Calvin and Keil. His "a line of descendants and not an
  individual" is answered from the Hebrew itself: elsewhere זֶרַע with singular
  forms names one descendant, at 3:15b it is "he" who strikes the serpent's own
  head, and the Greek translator read one person (Collins, Alexander, Leupold).
  That answer is `disputed` too, on Keil, and Collins claims for it only that
  the syntax is "quite consistent with" one person. The scene read whole
  answers him too: the serpent speaks and twists God's command, as no animal
  does of itself; the blow falls on the serpent itself; and God sets the
  enmity; so the sentence is a promise of victory over the power behind the
  serpent (Collins, Woudstra, Keil). Its step is `plausible`, and the ground it
  turns on, that an evil power stands behind the serpent, is `disputed` on
  Westermann. The readers before Christ do not read the verse so: Jubilees,
  Philo and Josephus read the serpent as an animal or an emblem. The fulfilment,
  with the syntax and the scene, can be defended, and so can Westermann.
  **Under the Scripture standard the fulfilment prevails**
  (`promise_turns_on_the_standard`): its grounds are all Scripture, and
  Westermann's dissent rests on his philology of "seed", so it is not heard.
  Under the evidence standard it is, and nothing prevails.
  `Dispute.PromiseHearing` reports both.
- **The Septuagint's "he"**, αὐτός for the neuter σπέρμα, may show that a
  Jewish translator before Christ read the promise of one person
  (`greekHeCase_establishes`), so that reading would be no Christian invention.
  Collins holds it; Philo, the earliest known reader of the Greek, took the
  masculine as a "barbarism" meaning the mind, and Lewis leaves it open, so it
  is `disputed`. It leaves the father open (`the_greek_he_leaves_the_father_open`): the same Greek
  calls the seed Hannah asks for "him", and that son has a father.

**Wegner's objection is encoded in its sharpest form, and the module shows the
circle in it rather than alleging one.** Wegner does not merely say that
עַלְמָה means "young woman". He says that הָרָה at Isaiah 7:14 is a predicate
adjective, so the clause reads "the עַלְמָה *is* pregnant" — already, when the
sign is given — and a pregnant woman is not a virgin; the one clear Isaianic
case then settles the word. `wegner_establishes` grants him every premise and
checks that the argument goes through, because a rival worth answering has to
be stated at full strength first.

The parse is not the weak point, and the encoding says so by granting it
throughout: Rydelnik — cited here through Postell, who reports him at 474 —
reads the same predicate adjective and draws the opposite conclusion, that the
virgin *is* pregnant and the sign is therefore as deep as Sheol. What the
grammar does not supply is that the pregnancy is an *ordinary* one, and that is
the premise that excludes virginity. `wegner_needs_ordinary_pregnancy` removes
it and the objection stops. `readingSuppliesOrdinaryPregnancy` then supplies it
the way Wegner's own case does — from the near-term reading of the sign — and
with the lexical conclusion turned back against that reading, the two legs
close. `circle_leaves_the_lexical_conclusion_open` and
`circle_leaves_the_denial_open` are the result: keep every uncontested datum,
and *neither* end is settled — not established, and not refuted either. A cycle
of implications is satisfied outright by a valuation on which all of its nodes
are false, and equally by one granting Wegner's own conclusion. Nothing enters
the loop, so nothing comes out of it, in either direction. That is a
demonstration rather than a complaint, and it is conditional in the usual way:
a defender of Wegner should deny `readingSuppliesOrdinaryPregnancy` and argue
that the near-term reading stands on the historical evidence alone.

Postell's second reply is independent of the first and survives that defence.
The other clear עַלְמָה passages Wegner himself lists are cases of virgins, so a
single referent cannot be what settles the denotation — the same principle
would settle it the other way. `usage_parity_blocks_wegner` checks it, and the
atom is marked `plausible` rather than `wellSupported` because Postell's "in
fact virgins" is stronger than Wegner's own discussion of Song 6:8.

**The oldest reply goes to the ordinary pregnancy itself.** Justin, Irenaeus
and Origen answer the near-term reading with one argument. The oracle promised a
*sign*, offered "in the depth or in the height" (7:11), and an ordinary
conception happens to every woman who is not barren, so it would be no sign.
Rydelnik makes the same move today. `signLine` encodes it, and it denies the one
ground of Wegner's objection that the grammar does not supply.
`sign_leaves_the_lexical_conclusion_open` measures what that buys: with the
fathers' grounds in place of the ordinary pregnancy, Wegner's lexical
conclusion is independent of what remains. The objection is blocked, and
nothing is shown about the word.

The rival is written first, and Wegner holds it himself: a sign need not be a
miracle. Isaiah's own children are "signs and portents" (8:18), and this sign
is dated by a child's infancy (7:16), so its point may be its timing. Rhodea
argues the same. `reply_leaves_the_pregnancy_open` shows that the reply blocks
the fathers in turn, without supplying Wegner's ordinary pregnancy.

`Dispute.Wegner` puts the three positions together. Every one of them has a
`disputed` weakest link, so the dispute ties (`nothing_prevails_over_wegner`).
Both the fathers alone and Wegner with the reply are defensible resolutions of
it. What would decide it is one of two ratings: whether the sign of 7:14 must be
the kind offered at 7:11, and whether the reply's inference survives Rydelnik,
who grants its grounds and denies its conclusion.

The critical case against the Isaianic strand is now *derived* rather than
assumed. `critical` used to carry `¬isaiahPredictsVirginBirth` as a bare
premise; it now carries the step that produces it — that a sign given for
Ahaz's generation is not also a prediction of a virgin conception — and
`criticalDenial_establishes` checks that the step works. Berry supplies the
objection: how Isaiah 7:14 was fulfilled in Ahaz's own day is itself an open
question, and `berry_blocks_critical_denial` shows that granting him that much
takes the exclusion out. It does no more than that. It does not establish the
predictive reading and it does not touch the lexical dispute.

Berry also supplies a *defensive* lexical premise — that the semantic range of
עַלְמָה does not exclude "virgin" — and `admissibility_is_not_enough` measures
what it is worth: nothing, on its own. *May mean* is not *does mean*, and the
whole Isaianic strand lives in that gap.

**The compositional strand** (Postell) declines the lexical fight altogether.
Isaiah 7 sits inside Isaiah 2–12, a unit framed by eschatological vision at
2:1–4 and 11:1–12:6; on the principle that an oracle's meaning in a finished
book is set by its literary placement rather than by the events it describes —
argued from the making of canonical Jeremiah — 7:14 anticipates a future,
miraculous birth. The hinge is `compositionGovernsMeaning`, and a reader who
holds that an oracle's historical setting fixes its sense rejects it outright.

Postell also supplies the module's sharpest rival-defeater. `parityDefeats`
`NearTermExclusion` observes that Isaiah 9:5–6 and 11:1–10 are read as messianic
without reservation *and* stand on the same near-term Assyrian timeline as 7:14
— the invasion of 8:7–8, the oppressor's rod of 10:5. So a near-term setting
cannot be what rules out messianic reference, or it would rule out 9 and 11 too.
`parity_blocks_critical_denial` checks it. Notably the Targum is cited *for*
this premise: it reads 9:5–6 and 11:1 messianically while declining to read 7:14
so, which makes it a hostile witness and therefore a strong one.

That gives the critical exclusion step two independent defeaters. Berry's is
evidential — we do not know how the sign was fulfilled in Ahaz's day. Postell's
is structural — the near-term setting was never the right kind of reason.

**Taken together, the positions make a dispute, and the dispute has an outcome
the entailment results cannot state.** `Dispute.lean` treats the scriptural
reading, the critical denial, Berry, Postell's two counterexamples and Motyer
as the nodes of an
argumentation framework and proves who defeats whom — a defeat being an attack
derived from entailment that the cited confidences do not block. Against the
scriptural reading alone, `nothing_prevails_unanswered`: the critical denial and
the scriptural reading defeat each other, because the weakest premise on each
side is `disputed` (`christian_defeats_critical`). Hear Berry and Postell, and
`scriptural_reading_prevails_once_replies_are_heard`: nothing defeats Postell's
counterexamples, they defeat the critic, and so they defend the scriptural
reading — and Berry, and Motyer with Compton — against the only party that
defeats them. The critic
is left with no defence at all (`critical_denial_indefensible`). Inference
steps are rated like premises, and Berry's and Motyer's are `disputed`, so
alone they tie with the critic: `nothing_prevails_on_motyer_alone`, and
`motyer_rests_on_his_inference` shows the weight of his reply is on that step.
The outcome turns on Postell's inference being `plausible` — no cited source
grants his grounds and keeps the exclusion. He gives two counterexamples, from
Isaiah 9 and 11 and from Micah 5; either suffices
(`scriptural_reading_prevails_without_postell`), and without both nothing
prevails (`nothing_prevails_without_the_counterexamples`). It turns too on the
critic's premises being `disputed`, as the replies, Motyer and Compton contest
them.

**Luke is a second witness to the conception, not to the prophecy.** His
account is parallel to Matthew's and independent of it, but it never quotes
Isaiah 7:14. Luke 1:31 is close to the Septuagint's wording, and whether that is
an allusion is disputed: `lukeAllusionEdge` records it as one, attributed, and
`annunciationFormEdge` records the rival reading, on which the wording is the
stock birth-announcement form that Isaiah 7:14 itself uses. Luke adds to
`independentAttestation`; he adds nothing to the rating of the predictive
reading.

`hinges_jointly_load_bearing` is the result worth having. No single interpretive
hinge carries the argument any more — strip *almah* and the other three strands
still deliver the criterion, which `almah_not_load_bearing` records. Strip all
four and the argument collapses. Genesis's strand delivers it only on Luther's
reading of its hinge, which nothing here forces
(`nothing_prevails_over_her_seed`). `almah_is_load_bearing_alone` keeps the
pre-Miravalle finding on the books: within the Isaianic strand taken by itself,
the lexical premise still carries everything.

**The magisterial strand is encoded separately and is not part of `christian`.**
Papal teaching on Mary's virginity in conceiving, as collated by Miravalle, is
a Roman Catholic premise; this library's author does not grant that magisterial
teaching settles doctrinal questions, and the encoding says so rather than
quietly folding it in. `catholic` is the package for a reader who does grant it.
`magisterial_authority_is_load_bearing` shows what follows for a reader who does
not: that route yields nothing on its own, and the four scriptural strands have
to carry the argument by themselves. The rival is cited to Westminster I.x.

Matthew's and Luke's birth narratives agree on the virgin conception while
differing in nearly every other detail, and that convergence is encoded as a
multiple-attestation premise — though the independence of the two traditions is
itself debated, and is marked `plausible` rather than `wellSupported`.

### Where things are

This argument is a directory, because at fourteen hundred lines it was one file
that no one could hold in view. The dependencies run one way. Where a file
outgrew three hundred lines of code, the material for the disputes over Wegner's
objection, over the Septuagint's word and over the woman's seed, and the
citations for the dispute over the critical denial, went into modules of their
own beside it.

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `Atoms.lean` | the `Claim` atoms, the recurring sources, the intertextual edges, the criterion |
| `Sources.lean` | `cite`: a citation and a classification for every atom |
| `Sources/Genesis.lean` | the citations of the dispute over the woman's seed |
| `Sources/NearTerm.lean` | the citations of the dispute over the critical denial |
| `Sources/Septuagint.lean` | the citations of the dispute over the Septuagint's word |
| `Sources/Versions.lean` | the Hebrew text of Qumran, the Syriac, and the referential reply |
| `Sources/Wegner.lean` | the citations of the dispute over Wegner's objection |
| `Lines.lean` | the inference steps, and the lines of reason they compose into |
| `Packages.lean` | the positions, and the variant packages the results refute |
| `Results.lean` | the `@[headline]` results about the strands, with their trust base |
| `Results/Wegner.lean` | the results about Wegner's objection, its circle, and the sign |
| `Results/Septuagint.lean` | what the Septuagint rests on, what it shows, and what it leaves open |
| `Results/Genesis.lean` | what "her seed" says of a father, read two ways, and the Greek's "he" |
| `Dispute.lean` | the critical denial, the scriptural reading and four replies as one dispute |
| `Dispute/Wegner.lean` | Wegner, the fathers' sign argument and the near-term reply as another |
| `Dispute/Septuagint.lean` | the Septuagint, Wegner, Rico and Gentry, and the laws, as a third |
| `Dispute/Genesis.lean` | Luther, Leupold and Lewis on "her seed", as a fourth |
| `Dispute/Protoevangelium.lean` | the promise fulfilled, and Westermann's denial, as a fifth |
| `Dispute/PromiseHearing.lean` | that dispute heard under each standard |

Shared material lives further out: passages and citation bundles in
`Testimony.Scripture`, the `Line` and `caseOf` vocabulary in
`Testimony.Logic.Line`, and the `establish` and `refute_with` tactics in
`Testimony.Logic.Tactic`.

## TestimonyArguments.BornOfAVirgin.Atoms — the atomic claims, and what cites them

The atoms this argument is built from, the `Source` shapes that recur across
them, the typed intertextual edges between the passages, and the criterion the
argument is about. Everything here is *what the argument is about*; nothing
here asserts anything.

See `TestimonyArguments.BornOfAVirgin` for the dispute this encodes.

#### Recurring sources

Five works carry this argument, and each carries several atoms at the same
pinpoint with the same confidence. Written out at every atom, the citation was
repeated rather than the claim — and a `Source` differing from its neighbour by
one field is hard to read as deliberate.

These are values, so an atom that cites one of them *with something further*
says so with `{ ... with supporting := ... }`, and the difference is the part a
reader sees.

<a id="motyerOnIsaiah"></a>
**`motyerOnIsaiah`**

Motyer on Isaiah 7:14: the predictive reading and the lexical premise it

```lean
def motyerOnIsaiah : Source :=
```

<a id="miravalleOnGenesis"></a>
**`miravalleOnGenesis`**

Miravalle on Genesis 3:15, in *Meet Your Mother*: the verse is the
"Protoevangelium", "the first reference to Jesus as the future Redeemer of the
world", and to speak of "the 'seed' of a woman rather than the seed of a man" is
"already a hint of Mary's virginal conception of Jesus". His word is "hint": a
remark in passing, not an argument from the Hebrew.

The protoevangelium strand rests on him and on Luther, the reader who argues
from the wording (`herSeedLine`); the Michean strand rests on Miravalle alone
(`miravalleOnMicah`). Every atom citing this is `disputed`.

```lean
def miravalleOnGenesis : Source :=
  { primary := Reference.work miravalleMeetYourMother,
    tradition := Tradition.romanCatholic, confidence := Confidence.disputed }
```

<a id="miravalleOnMicah"></a>
**`miravalleOnMicah`**

Miravalle on Micah 5:2–3, in *Introduction to Mary*: the mother "so
specifically designated without a husband" conveys "the same virginal sense as
we see in Isaiah 7:14". The passage is on page 18 of the 1993 printing; the
library's entry is the 2020 printing, whose page could not be checked, so the
book is cited whole.

```lean
def miravalleOnMicah : Source :=
  { primary := Reference.work miravalleIntroductionToMary,
    tradition := Tradition.romanCatholic, confidence := Confidence.disputed }
```

#### Intertextual edges and readings

<a id="quotationEdge"></a>
**`quotationEdge`**

Matthew explicitly quotes Isaiah, via the Septuagint's παρθένος.

```lean
def quotationEdge : IntertextEdge :=
  { fromPassage := Scripture.matthew1_23, toPassage := Scripture.isaiah7_14,
    relation := RelationType.quotation,
    source := Scripture.na28Apparatus Scripture.matthew1_23 }
```

<a id="protoevangeliumEdge"></a>
**`protoevangeliumEdge`**

Genesis 3:15 read as promise rather than quotation. Typed as `.promise`,
not `.prediction`: what Miravalle argues is that the protoevangelium *commits*
to a redeemer born of a woman, and collapsing that into a prediction would beg
the question the Michean and Isaianic strands are also asking.

```lean
def protoevangeliumEdge : IntertextEdge :=
  { fromPassage := Scripture.matthew1_23, toPassage := Scripture.genesis3_15,
    relation := RelationType.promise,
    source := miravalleOnGenesis }
```

<a id="micahMaternalEdge"></a>
**`micahMaternalEdge`**

Micah 5:3's maternal reference, read as a messianic theme rather than a
verbal link — there is no quotation of Micah 5:3 in the birth narratives.

```lean
def micahMaternalEdge : IntertextEdge :=
  { fromPassage := Scripture.matthew1_23, toPassage := Scripture.micah5_3,
    relation := RelationType.messianicTheme,
    source := miravalleOnMicah }
```

<a id="lukeAllusionEdge"></a>
**`lukeAllusionEdge`**

**Luke's annunciation, read as an allusion to Isaiah 7:14.** Luke never
quotes the verse, but Luke 1:31 is close to its Septuagint wording, and Luke
1:27 and 1:32 bring in the house and the throne of David, as Isaiah 7:13 and
9:6–7 do. Whether that is an allusion is disputed, and both sides are recorded
here: Davies and Allison find an influence from Isaiah 7:14, Fitzmyer rejects
it, as Rhodea reports (71 n. 66). Typed `.allusion`, never `.quotation`: that
is the difference between Luke and Matthew. See `annunciationFormEdge` for the
rival reading of the same wording.

```lean
def lukeAllusionEdge : IntertextEdge :=
  { fromPassage := Scripture.luke1_31, toPassage := Scripture.isaiah7_14,
    relation := RelationType.allusion,
    source :=
      { primary := Reference.work rhodeaDidMatthewConceive (Bib.Locus.page 71),
        supporting :=
          [Reference.scripture
              [Scripture.verseIn TextualTradition.nestleAland28
                  Scripture.luke1_31,
                Scripture.verseIn TextualTradition.septuagint
                  Scripture.isaiah7_14]],
        tradition := Tradition.christianHistoricalGrammatical,
        confidence := Confidence.disputed } }
```

<a id="annunciationFormEdge"></a>
**`annunciationFormEdge`**

**The rival reading: the wording is the birth-announcement form.** Luke 1:31
is as close to the announcement to Hagar (Gen 16:11) as to Isaiah 7:14, and
Isaiah 7:14 is itself an instance of the form, which Brown and others trace
through Ishmael, Isaac, Samson, John and Jesus (Johnson 270 n. 6; Young 113–14).
On this reading the shared wording is shared form, not dependence — typed
`.thematic`.

```lean
def annunciationFormEdge : IntertextEdge :=
  { fromPassage := Scripture.luke1_31, toPassage := Scripture.genesis16_11,
    relation := RelationType.thematic,
    source :=
      { primary := Reference.work johnsonSamsonTypeScene (Bib.Locus.page 270),
        supporting :=
          [Reference.work youngImmanuelProphecy (Bib.Locus.pages 113 114),
            Reference.work brownProblemVirginalConception (Bib.Locus.page 31)],
        tradition := Tradition.criticalScholarship,
        confidence := Confidence.wellSupported } }
```

The Christian predictive reading of Isaiah 7:14. Far more contested than

Miravalle's reading of Micah 5:2–3: the oracle names a mother and no

<a id="bornOfAVirgin"></a>
**`bornOfAVirgin`**

The criterion this argument establishes a candidate must meet.

```lean
def bornOfAVirgin : FulfillmentCriterion :=
  { name := "born of a virgin", basis := predictiveReading }
```

## TestimonyArguments.BornOfAVirgin.Sources.Genesis — the citations of the dispute over "her seed"

The atoms of the dispute over what the wording of Genesis 3:15 says about a
father: whether "her seed" signifies a birth without one, or fits such a birth
once it has happened, what else might explain the wording, and what the Greek's
"he" adds. Cited here and dispatched from `cite` by name, for the reason
`Sources.Wegner` gives.

Luther, Leupold, Keil and Calvin are cited from their commentaries, Lewis and
Collins from their articles, Henry by passage, and Akin from the publisher's
site. Martin is cited whole: the library has not read his article, and quotes
him only as Collins does.

<a id="wordingSignifiesAFatherlessBirthCited"></a>
**`wordingSignifiesAFatherlessBirthCited`**

`wordingSignifiesAFatherlessBirth`. Luther makes the argument from the
wording: "Thus women continued to bring forth until the Flood; and afterwards
also, until the time of Mary. But the seed of none of those women could truly be
said to be the Seed of the woman, but might rather be said to have been the seed
of the man. But that which was born from Mary was conceived of the Holy Ghost
and was the true Seed of Mary" (*Luther on the Creation* 298–99). Henry: "He was
likewise to be the seed of a woman only, of a virgin" (on 3:15). Akin finds in
the wording "a hint of the Virgin Birth".

Luther finds the sense in the words of Genesis, and holds that Isaiah later
"threw some additional light upon this glorious promise ... For it was then made
certain that this Seed would not be born from the union of a man and a woman"
(298). Irenaeus reads the verse of the Virgin's son, "He who should be born of a
woman, [namely] from the Virgin" (*Against Heresies* V.21.1), though he does not
argue from the wording.

`disputed`: Leupold and Keil, who read the verse as the promise of Christ, deny
that the wording says this (`posterityLine`); Calvin gives both of their grounds
(170) without discussing the point; and Lewis denies it from what Genesis says
of Hagar and Rebekah (`idiomLine`).

```lean
def wordingSignifiesAFatherlessBirthCited : AtomMeta :=
  {
    label :=
      "The wording 'her seed' itself signifies a birth with no human father",
    kind := PremiseKind.interpretive,
    source :=
      { primary := Reference.work lutherOnTheCreation (Bib.Locus.pages 298 299),
        supporting :=
          [Reference.work henryCommentary
              (Bib.Locus.adLoc Scripture.genesis3_15),
            Reference.work akinWomanSeedSerpent],
        tradition := Tradition.christianTypological,
        confidence := Confidence.disputed } }
```

<a id="wordingFitsAFatherlessBirthCited"></a>
**`wordingFitsAFatherlessBirthCited`**

`wordingFitsAFatherlessBirth`. Leupold, asked whether the expression is "so
phrased in reference to Mary and the virgin birth": "Not primarily, but at least
incidentally"; "an expression is chosen that meets with literal fulfilment in
Him who is virgin born and not of the seed of man.
Yet we prefer to state the case thus: the expression used does not specifically
prophesy the virgin birth, but it coincides and agrees with it under divine
providence" (169). Keil: "in the fact that the destroyer of the serpent was born
of a woman (without a human father) they were fulfilled in a way which showed
that the promise must have proceeded from that Being, who secured its
fulfilment not only in its essential force, but even in its apparently casual
form" (102).

`disputed`, because it presupposes the virginal conception, which this argument
rates `disputed` (`maryConceivedAsVirgin`). Among readers who grant that
conception, none found denies the fit: Leupold and Keil, who deny that the
wording signifies it, grant this.

```lean
def wordingFitsAFatherlessBirthCited : AtomMeta :=
  {
    label :=
      "The wording 'her seed' fits a birth with no human father, as fulfilled in Christ",
    kind := PremiseKind.interpretive,
    source :=
      { primary := Reference.work leupoldGenesis (Bib.Locus.page 169),
        supporting :=
          [Reference.work keilDelitzschPentateuch (Bib.Locus.page 102)],
        tradition := Tradition.christianHistoricalGrammatical,
        confidence := Confidence.disputed } }
```

<a id="seedIsHerPosterityFirstCited"></a>
**`seedIsHerPosterityFirstCited`**

`seedIsHerPosterityFirst`. Leupold: "the expression 'her seed' in its first
meaning is a collective noun and includes all who are enrolled in the struggle
against Satan, without being themselves virgin born" (169) — not every
descendant, for "within the circle of the broadest possible meaning of zéra' must
be drawn a circle quite a bit smaller" (167). Calvin: "for who will concede that
a collective noun is to be understood of one man only? ... I explain, therefore,
the seed to mean the posterity of the woman generally" (170). Keil: "It does not
follow from this, however, apart from other considerations, that by the seed of
the woman we are to understand one solitary person, one individual only" (101).

`disputed`. Collins argues that the Hebrew's syntax is "quite consistent with the
pattern where a single individual is in view" (145), and that on a "bottom-up"
reading of the final form "it would be fair to read this as God's threat to the
snake, of an individual who will engage the snake in combat and win" (146).

```lean
def seedIsHerPosterityFirstCited : AtomMeta :=
  {
    label :=
```

<a id="womanNamedForTheDeceptionCited"></a>
**`womanNamedForTheDeceptionCited`**

`womanNamedForTheDeception`. Leupold: "The woman, as one factor in the
enmity, is stressed to the exclusion of man because the woman was beguiled"
(165); "the one tempted and brought to fall is chosen by God to produce the one
that is to bring Satan to fall" (169). Calvin: "He mentions the woman on this
account, because, as she had yielded to the subtlety of the devil, and being
first deceived, had drawn her husband into the participation of her ruin, so she
had peculiar need of consolation" (170). Henry: "God does the woman the honour to
call him rather her seed, because she it was whom the devil had beguiled". Keil
allows it — "even if the words had reference first of all to the fact that the
woman had been led astray by the serpent" — and gives his own reason in the same
key: "as it was through the woman that the craft of the devil brought sin and
death into the world, so it is also through the woman that the grace of God will
give to the fallen human race the conqueror" (102).

`wellSupported`: Lutheran, Reformed and Puritan readers give it, Henry among
them, who also holds that the wording signifies a birth from a virgin. No reader
found denies it.

```lean
def womanNamedForTheDeceptionCited : AtomMeta
```

`womansSeedSaidOfOrdinaryBirths`. What the Hebrew reads: the angel promises

family blesses her seed, זַרְעֵךְ, to possess the gate of its enemies (24:60).

Hebrew to describe descendants by the noun zeraʿ, it is unusual (though not
unique) to use the term with a feminine possessive pronoun" (299). Scripture

<a id="lxxCallsTheSeedHeCited"></a>
**`lxxCallsTheSeedHeCited`**

`lxxCallsTheSeedHe`. What the Greek reads, from Rahlfs's text: καὶ ἀνὰ μέσον
τοῦ σπέρματος αὐτῆς· αὐτός σου τηρήσει κεφαλήν, "and between her seed: he will
watch for your head". The pronoun αὐτός is masculine, and σπέρμα is neuter.
Collins: "The mismatch in gender between pronoun and antecedent is held to be
evidence that the LXX translator saw this as a prophecy of a specific
individual" (141). `consensus`: no one denies the reading.

```lean

  {
    label :=
      "The Greek of Genesis 3:15 calls the woman's seed 'he', though σπέρμα is neuter",
    kind := PremiseKind.textual,
    source :=
      {
        primary :=
          Reference.scripture
            [Scripture.verseIn TextualTradition.septuagint
                Scripture.genesis3_15],

        tradition := Tradition.criticalScholarship,
        confidence := Confidence.consensus } }
```

<a id="lxxReadsOneDescendantCited"></a>
**`lxxReadsOneDescendantCited`**

`lxxReadsOneDescendant`. Collins: "The evidence of the Greek translators
makes it beyond question that the translator of Genesis 3:15 meant to convey
that an individual was promised" (145). The reading "is generally acknowledged"
(141), and Martin's article is its usual citation: as Collins quotes him, Martin
calls the Greek "the earliest evidence of an individual messianic
interpretation" (Collins 141 n. 4). Elsewhere the Greek translators use a
masculine pronoun after the neuter σπέρμα when one person is meant: αὐτόν at 1
Samuel 1:11, and ὅς, αὐτός and αὐτόν at 2 Samuel 7:12–14 (Collins 144).

`disputed`, on Philo, the earliest known reader of this Greek. He grants that
it says "he", and reads it as a "barbarism" that is correct in meaning, of the
mind and not of a person: "the woman is not he, but she", and "the mind is
masculine" (*Allegorical Interpretation* III.188). Lewis leaves the question
open: "Sperma is a neuter noun in Greek and would have taken a neuter pronoun had
the translators not thought of an individual", but the masculine "could be an
oversight … it is possible that the translator reveals a messianic
understanding—which, if true, would then be the earliest known" (300). John Day
is reported to call it "simply an over-literal translation of the Hebrew"; his
words could not be read, and he is not counted. The doubt Collins reports is
about the Hebrew, not the Greek (141).

```lean
def lxxReadsOneDescendantCited : AtomMeta
```

woman".

individual is in view. `disputed`: Collins answers Westermann that the woman's

also used in reference to an individual and not only in the collective sense"
(168); Alexander, that the seed "must be understood as referring to a single
individual" (363); Hamilton, that "the text switches from a collective referent
to a singular one" (32). `syntaxLine` gives their argument.

## TestimonyArguments.BornOfAVirgin.Sources.NearTerm — the citations of the near-term dispute

The atoms of the dispute over the critical denial, cited here and dispatched
from `cite` by name: the critic's two premises, that 7:14 was a near-term sign
to Ahaz and that such a sign excludes a messianic sense, and the grounds of the
replies to them — Berry's, Postell's Micah counterexample, and Motyer's with
Compton's. (Postell's Isaiah counterexample rests on atoms the compositional
strand also uses, and is cited with them in `Sources.lean`.)

They sit apart for the reason `Sources.Wegner` does: `cite` stays one total
function, and each value below is reached from exactly one of its cases.

<a id="isaiahIsNearTermSignToAhazCited"></a>
**`isaiahIsNearTermSignToAhazCited`**

`isaiahIsNearTermSignToAhaz`. The reading Justin already answers, in Trypho's
form: fulfilled in Hezekiah (Dial. 67, 77). Origen's reply is a question — which
child of Ahaz's day was called Immanuel? — and his conclusion that the sign was
given to the house of David (Cels. I.35). Motyer denies it most directly (1970,
120, 124): the sign confirms events after the fact, and Maher-shalal-hash-baz,
not Immanuel, carries the timetable. So does Compton (2007, 12): 7:14 is
addressed to the house of David, in plural pronouns, and only 7:15–16, with a
singular "you", to Ahaz. `disputed` for that reason, on the definition that
re-rated the exclusion premise.

```lean
def isaiahIsNearTermSignToAhazCited : AtomMeta :=
  {
    label :=
      "Isaiah 7:14 is a near-term sign to Ahaz, fulfilled in Isaiah's generation",
    kind := PremiseKind.interpretive,
    source := brownOnBirth Confidence.disputed }
```

<a id="nearTermExcludesMessianicSenseCited"></a>
**`nearTermExcludesMessianicSenseCited`**

`nearTermExcludesMessianicSense`. The premise Berry and Postell deny, and
Motyer with them: `disputed` by the library's own definition, since the contest
is recorded in `berryLine` and `postellLine`. It was once cited `wellSupported`
on Brown's authority, which let the critic outrank both replies. Compton (2007,
12–14) denies it on a third ground: the near-term part of the oracle, 7:15–16,
uses the child's infancy only as a measure of time, and so does not need the
child born in Ahaz's day.

```lean
def nearTermExcludesMessianicSenseCited : AtomMeta :=
  {
    label :=
      "A sign given for Ahaz's generation is not also a prediction of a virgin birth",
    kind := PremiseKind.interpretive,
    source := brownOnBirth Confidence.disputed }
```

## TestimonyArguments.BornOfAVirgin.Sources.Septuagint — the citations of the Septuagint dispute

The atoms of the dispute over what the Septuagint's παρθένος shows, cited here
and dispatched from `cite` by name: when and by whom the Greek Isaiah was made,
what its word for the woman of 7:14 meant, the evidence each side reads, and
what the translator can be taken to have meant.

They sit apart for the reason `Sources.Wegner` does: `cite` stays one total
function, and each value below is reached from exactly one of its cases.

Rico and Gentry are cited from their book; Bratcher, Walton, Wegner, Rhodea and
Postell from their articles; Davidson from his dictionary article; Meade from
his comment on his own blog post. Three readings are known to the library only
through the scholar who reports them, and each comment says so: Delling's and
Tsevat's, through Rhodea, and Gray's, through Bratcher.

<a id="lxxIsPreChristianCited"></a>
**`lxxIsPreChristianCited`**

`lxxIsPreChristian`. Irenaeus makes the argument from it: Isaiah 7:14 "was
interpreted into Greek by the Jews themselves, much before the period of our
Lord's advent, that there might remain no suspicion that perchance the Jews,
complying with our humour, did put this interpretation upon these words"
(*Against Heresies* III.21.1). Justin presses Trypho with the version made by
"the seventy elders who were with Ptolemy" (*Dialogue* 71). Chrysostom makes the
same point: the Seventy, "as having entered upon this work an hundred years or
more before the coming of Christ, stand clear from all such suspicion" (*Homilies
on Matthew* 5); Eusebius adds that they were "men of Hebrew race, experts in the
accuracy of their knowledge of their national language" (*Dem. Ev.* VII.1). The
rival grants the date: Wegner puts the translator "about 250–150 BC" (483).
`consensus`.

```lean
def lxxIsPreChristianCited : AtomMeta
```

<a id="parthenosMeansVirginCited"></a>
**`parthenosMeansVirginCited`**

`parthenosMeansVirgin`. Rico and Gentry: "There is no doubt that we should
take the term parthenos to mean 'virgin' whenever it appears in Semitic Koine
Greek: the example of Gn 34:1–3 is the exception that proves the rule" (21).
Postell reports that they "insist" on it (472 n. 45). Bratcher reaches the same
conclusion from the Septuagint's usage, without their argument: "parthenos
definitely means 'virgin' in the LXX; only very exceptionally (and, inexplicably,
in Gen. 34:3) is it used otherwise" (113).

`disputed`, because scholars this argument cites deny it. Wegner holds that in
the translator's day the word meant "a young woman of marriageable age", and
came to mean "virgin" only by the time of the New Testament (482–83). Walton:
"Therefore the LXX is not necessarily betraying an interpretation as virgin by
choosing this term" (293). Rhodea: "in the LXX, παρθένος need not refer to a
virgo intacta" (67). Meade: "παρθενος simply means young woman in this verse and
in other places in the LXX" (comment of 9 January 2013).

```lean

  { label := "In the Greek of the Septuagint, παρθένος means a virgin",
    kind := PremiseKind.linguistic,

        supporting :=
          [Reference.work bratcherStudyOfIsaiah (Bib.Locus.page 113),
            Reference.work postellIsaiahMessianic (Bib.Locus.page 472)],
        tradition := Tradition.christianHistoricalGrammatical,
        confidence := Confidence.disputed } }
```

<a id="parthenosMeantYoungWomanCited"></a>
**`parthenosMeantYoungWomanCited`**

`parthenosMeantYoungWoman`. A claim about the word, not about any woman: in
the translator's Greek, παρθένος meant "young woman", and did not yet mean
"virgin". Wegner and Walton grant that by the New Testament it meant "virgin";
Meade and Davidson put that sense down to Christian use. The dispute is over the
translator's day, two or three centuries before Matthew.

Wegner: "In early Greek literature it appears to have had the meaning of 'a young
woman of marriageable age' (with or without the focus on virginity), but by NT
times this word developed the more technical meaning of 'virgin'" (482). So the
translator of Isaiah chose a word for a young woman, "an excellent word choice to
convey what the LXX's author meant", and "in the intervening time between the
LXX and the NT book of Matthew, the word παρθένος changed in meaning" (483).
Rhodea follows him, with an "apparently" (67). Meade holds it too: παρθένος
"simply means young woman in this verse and in other places in the LXX", and by
the time of Justin it had been "hijacked or used to mean 'chaste woman' only"
(comment of 9 January 2013). `disputed`: Rico and Gentry deny it, and so does
Bratcher.

```lean
def parthenosMeantYoungWomanCited : AtomMeta :=
  {
    label :=
      "In the Septuagint's day, παρθένος meant 'young woman'; not yet 'virgin'",
    kind := PremiseKind.linguistic,
    source :=
      have __src :=
        wegnerOnAlmah (Bib.Locus.pages 482 483)
          Confidence.disputed;
      { primary := __src.primary,
        supporting :=
          [Reference.work rhodeaDidMatthewConceive (Bib.Locus.page 67),
            Reference.work meadeAncientVersionsComment],
        tradition := __src.tradition, confidence := __src.confidence } }
```

<a id="earlyGreekParthenosIsYoungWomanCited"></a>
**`earlyGreekParthenosIsYoungWomanCited`**

`earlyGreekParthenosIsYoungWoman`. Wegner (482) and Rhodea (67) both state it
from BDAG 777: "a young woman of marriageable age, with or without focus on
virginity". BDAG itself gives that as the word's general use "Hom.+", from
Homer on, and sets against it the sense "in our lit.", the New Testament and the
early Christian writings: "one who has never engaged in sexual intercourse,
virgin". So the contrast in BDAG is between bodies of writing, not between
periods; "early Greek" is Wegner's and Rhodea's narrowing of it, and the claim
here is no more than the narrowing. BDAG gives no sense for the Septuagint.
LSJ, for classical Greek: "maiden, girl", "virgin, opp. γυνή", and "of unmarried
women who are not virgins" (1339). Walton: the word "does not always mean 'virgin' in
classical Greek" (293). Bratcher, who holds the opposite of Wegner about the
Septuagint, grants it: "at first the word was used in a general sense of
'girl', 'young woman', without any specific connotation of virginity" (112).
`wellSupported`: Rico and Gentry grant the older usage too, and explain Genesis
34:3 by it, as an "almost anachronistic use of the word parthenos" that
"corresponds to the general tendency of language in the Septuagint version of
the Pentateuch", whose language is "more elevated and classical than the
language of the later texts" (18). What they deny is that the older usage is the
Septuagint's at large.

```lean
def earlyGreekParthenosIsYoungWomanCited : AtomMeta
```

<a id="lawsUseParthenosAsVirginCited"></a>
**`lawsUseParthenosAsVirginCited`**

`lawsUseParthenosAsVirgin`. Bratcher makes the argument from the Greek of
the laws: in Deuteronomy 22 the Hebrew's בְּתוּלִים "stands concretely for 'tokens
of virginity' (LXX partheneia)", and in Leviticus 21 "the young woman so
characterized is clearly a virgin (LXX parthenos)" (102, where "Lev. 21:3" is a
misprint for 21:13); "The use of the cognates of parthenos in the LXX bears out
the conclusion that parthenos is 'virgin'", and "All this indicates that
parthenos is 'virgin' in the exact sense of the word" (113).

These are not uses of the word *of* a virgin, which would show nothing about its
sense: Walton observes that a thousand uses of "fiancée" of virgins would not
make it mean "virgin" (292). In these laws virginity is what the law turns on.
The priest's παρθένος is set against the widow, the woman put away, the defiled
woman and the harlot, and stands for "a woman in her virginity". The bride's τὰ
παρθένια are the tokens whose absence proves her a harlot, and Walton's own test
is that a word meaning "virgin" should have an abstract meaning "virginity"
(292).

`disputed`, as its step is, on Miller (`lawsLine` gives his dissent, and where
it breaks).

## TestimonyArguments.BornOfAVirgin.Sources.Versions — the Hebrew, the Syriac, and a reply

Three citations that say more than a label can: what the oldest Hebrew copy of
Isaiah reads at 7:14, what the Syriac Peshitta reads and what can be said of who
wrote it, and the reply to the lexical objection that leaves the word's sense
aside, with the fathers who made it. Cited here and dispatched from `cite` by
name, for the reason `Sources.Wegner` gives.

<a id="qumranConfirmsAlmahCited"></a>
**`qumranConfirmsAlmahCited`**

`qumranConfirmsAlmah`. What the oldest Hebrew copy of Isaiah reads. 1QIsaᵃ,
column VI, line 29, has הנה העלמה הרה, as the Masoretic Text has it: read in
Abegg's transcription, from Ulrich and Flint's text. The verse has other
variants — יהוה for אדני, and וקרא, "and one shall call", for וקראת, "and she
shall call" — but none at the word. 4QIsaˡ, the one other Qumran copy of the
verse, preserves too little of it to witness either way. The scroll is dated by
radiocarbon to 335–122 BC at one standard deviation, and by its hand to 150–125
BC (Jull et al. 14, 19).

So the Hebrew that both sides read is the Hebrew read before Christ, and neither
Christians nor their opponents changed the word. That settles the text, not the
sense: the scroll has the same word, and what it means is the dispute.
`consensus`.

```lean
def qumranConfirmsAlmahCited : AtomMeta
```

<a id="peshittaRendersBtultaCited"></a>
**`peshittaRendersBtultaCited`**

`peshittaRendersBtulta`. What the Syriac reads, and nothing about who wrote it
or why. Van der Kooij prints the reading (271). It is the Peshitta's only ܒܬܘܠܬܐ
for עַלְמָה: at Genesis 24:43, Exodus 2:8, Psalm 68:26 and Song 1:3 and 6:8 it
writes the cognate ܥܠܝܡܬܐ. Who made the version is disputed: Jews, for Bloch
("a work of Jewish hands outside of Palestine", 218 n.), or a Jewish Christian
who knew the Greek Isaiah, for van der Kooij (276–77, 287). Whether its 7:14 is
the translator's own reading, follows the Septuagint, or was changed later, Chen
finds impossible to settle: its agreement with the Greek "prevents us from
drawing any certain conclusion" (104–5). So it is cited for what it reads, and
not as a Jewish witness to "virgin". `consensus`, for the reading.

```lean
def peshittaRendersBtultaCited : AtomMeta
```

<a id="maryFitsIsaianicDescriptionCited"></a>
**`maryFitsIsaianicDescriptionCited`**

`maryFitsIsaianicDescription`. The referential reply: Mary was a young woman
of marriageable age and a virgin, so she answers Isaiah's description whatever
עַלְמָה denotes. France on Matthew 1:23, with Rico and Gentry.

The fathers gave the same answer to the Jewish "young woman", where they granted
it. Cyril of Alexandria: "κἂν εἰ λέγοιτο νεᾶνις ἡ παρθένος, οὐκ ἔξω κείσεται τοῦ
εἶναι παρθένος", even if the virgin were called a young woman, she will not cease
to be a virgin (PG 70, 204B). Cyril of Jerusalem: "though I assent to what they
say, even so I find the truth" (*Catechetical Lectures* 12.21). Eusebius: Christ's
entry by birth "as I and the Septuagint interpret it, of a virgin, or even
according to the current Jewish rendering, of a young woman" (*Dem. Ev.* VII.1).
Each, with Chrysostom (*Homilies on Matthew* 5), points to Deuteronomy 22, where
the betrothed νεᾶνις of 22:24–27 is the παῖς παρθένος of 22:23.

```lean
def maryFitsIsaianicDescriptionCited : AtomMeta
```

## TestimonyArguments.BornOfAVirgin.Sources.Wegner — the citations of the sign dispute

The atoms of the dispute over Wegner's objection, cited here and dispatched from
`cite` by name. They are the parse of הָרָה, the pregnancy it reports, what that
pregnancy is taken to show, and the fathers' sign argument against it with the
near-term reply to that.

They sit apart because `cite` is one total function over every atom. It keeps
that guarantee: each value below is reached from exactly one of its cases, so an
atom still cannot go uncited. What moves is only where the citation is written,
which keeps `Sources.lean` short enough to read.

<a id="harahIsPredicateAdjectiveCited"></a>
**`harahIsPredicateAdjectiveCited`**

`harahIsPredicateAdjective`. Deliberately not the contested step, and granted
throughout. Wegner puts it at "most likely" and cites Williams' grammar §75;
Rydelnik parses the clause exactly the same way and draws the opposite conclusion
from it, that the virgin *is* pregnant and the sign is therefore as deep as Sheol
(Isa 7:11).

```lean
def harahIsPredicateAdjectiveCited : AtomMeta :=
  {
    label :=
      "הָרָה at Isaiah 7:14 is a predicate adjective: the עַלְמָה is pregnant",
    kind := PremiseKind.linguistic,
    source :=
      have __src :=
        wegnerOnAlmah (Bib.Locus.page 471)
          Confidence.wellSupported;
      { primary := __src.primary,
        supporting :=
          [Reference.work postellIsaiahMessianic (Bib.Locus.page 474),
            Reference.work youngImmanuelProphecy (Bib.Locus.pages 115 116)],
        tradition := __src.tradition, confidence := __src.confidence } }
```

<a id="isaianicAlmahIsAlreadyPregnantCited"></a>
**`isaianicAlmahIsAlreadyPregnantCited`**

`isaianicAlmahIsAlreadyPregnant`. Granted on both sides of the dispute over
this verse: Wegner reads a present pregnancy and so does Rydelnik. What they
disagree about is what kind of pregnancy it is.

```lean
def isaianicAlmahIsAlreadyPregnantCited : AtomMeta :=
  {
    label :=
      "The עַלְמָה of Isaiah 7:14 is already pregnant when the sign is given",
    kind := PremiseKind.interpretive,
    source :=
      have __src :=
        wegnerOnAlmah (Bib.Locus.pages 471 472)
          Confidence.wellSupported;

        tradition := __src.tradition, confidence := __src.confidence } }
```

<a id="pregnancyAtTheSignIsOrdinaryCited"></a>
**`pregnancyAtTheSignIsOrdinaryCited`**

`pregnancyAtTheSignIsOrdinary`. The hinge of Wegner's objection, and not a
lexical claim at all. He gets it from the near-term reading of the sign: the
child born within nine months, everything in the oracle discharged by 701 BC.
Rydelnik, parsing הָרָה as Wegner does, denies it outright. So do the fathers, on
the ground that an ordinary conception would be no sign, and `signLine` is that
argument.

```lean
def pregnancyAtTheSignIsOrdinaryCited : AtomMeta :=
  { label := "The pregnancy Isaiah 7:14 announces is an ordinary conception",
    kind := PremiseKind.interpretive,
    source :=
      have __src :=
        wegnerOnAlmah (Bib.Locus.pages 476 478)
          Confidence.disputed;
      { primary := __src.primary,
        supporting :=
          [Reference.work postellIsaiahMessianic (Bib.Locus.page 474)],
        tradition := __src.tradition, confidence := __src.confidence } }
```

<a id="isaianicAlmahIsNotAVirginCited"></a>
**`isaianicAlmahIsNotAVirginCited`**

`isaianicAlmahIsNotAVirgin`. Wegner's conclusion about the referent. Postell
states the step it rests on baldly: "since the עַלְמָה in Isaiah 7:14 is already
pregnant, she obviously cannot be a virgin" (468).

```lean
def isaianicAlmahIsNotAVirginCited : AtomMeta :=

```

<a id="oneReferentSettlesDenotationCited"></a>
**`oneReferentSettlesDenotationCited`**

`oneReferentSettlesDenotation`. Wegner's method: Isaiah 7:14 is used as proof
that the word cannot mean "virgin". Rico and Gentry deny the principle — "the
analysis of the Immanuel oracle does not by itself allow one to draw a conclusion
concerning the meaning of the word" — and hold that the other occurrences settle
it the other way (quoted at Postell 468 n. 22).

```lean
def oneReferentSettlesDenotationCited : AtomMeta :=
  {
    label :=
      "What the עַלְמָה of Isaiah 7:14 turns out to be settles what the word denotes",
```

<a id="otherClearAlmahCasesAreVirginsCited"></a>
**`otherClearAlmahCasesAreVirginsCited`**

`otherClearAlmahCasesAreVirgins`. Postell at 468 n. 22, of the three passages
Wegner calls clearest. Marked `plausible` rather than `wellSupported` because it
is stronger than Wegner's own text: Genesis 24:43 is uncontested, but Wegner's
discussion of Song 6:8 allows that some of the עֲלָמוֹת in the harem would not be
virgins.

```lean
def otherClearAlmahCasesAreVirginsCited : AtomMeta
```

<a id="signMustBeExtraordinaryCited"></a>
**`signMustBeExtraordinaryCited`**

`signMustBeExtraordinary`. Origen's form of it: "What kind of sign, then,
would that have been — a young woman who was not a virgin giving birth to a
child?", tied to the sign offered "in the depth or in the height" (Cels. I.35).
Justin (Dial. 84) and Irenaeus (Haer. III.21.6) argue the same, and so does every
other father the library has read on the verse:

- Tertullian: a young woman's pregnancy, "a daily occurrence", "cannot possibly
  seem anything of a sign" (*Answer to the Jews* 9);
- Eusebius (*Dem. Ev.* VII.1);
- Cyril of Jerusalem: "the sign certainly must be something astonishing" (*Cat.*
  12.22);
- Chrysostom: "that which is a sign must of course be beyond the course of
  common events" (*Hom. Matt.* 5);
- Jerome: the sign "novum debet esse atque mirabile", must be new and wonderful
  (on 7:14, PL 24, 107D);
- Cyril of Alexandria (PG 70, 204C);
- Theodoret: "Οὐδεὶς δὲ σημεῖον καλεῖ τὸ καθ' ἑκάστην γινόμενον ἡμέραν", no
  one calls a sign what happens every day (PG 81, 276D).

Rydelnik makes the move today, as Postell reports (474).

`disputed`, though the fathers are unanimous: a rating says whether competent
readers contest a claim now, and two do. Wegner grants that the sign offered at
7:11 would have been miraculous, but holds that a sign may be an everyday
occurrence and reads the one given at 7:14, after Ahaz refused the first, as one
(469–470, 477–478); Rhodea holds that a sign does not require a miracle, and
that 7:11 does not make this one (64 and n. 10).

```lean
def signMustBeExtraordinaryCited : AtomMeta
```

<a id="ordinaryConceptionIsNoMarvelCited"></a>
**`ordinaryConceptionIsNoMarvelCited`**

`ordinaryConceptionIsNoMarvel`. Irenaeus: "what great thing or what sign
should have been in this, that a young woman conceiving by a man should bring
forth — a thing which happens to all women that produce offspring?" Justin asks
why God would give "a sign which is not common to all the first-born sons"
(Dial. 84). `consensus`, because the rival grants it: its point is that the
sign need not be a marvel, not that an ordinary conception is one (Rhodea
64).

```lean
def ordinaryConceptionIsNoMarvelCited : AtomMeta :=
  {
    label :=
      "An ordinary conception is nothing extraordinary: it happens to all women",
    kind := PremiseKind.interpretive,
    source :=
      {
        primary :=
          Reference.work irenaeusAgainstHeresies
            (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "III.21.6"),
        supporting :=
          [Reference.work justinDialogue (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "84"),
            Reference.work rhodeaDidMatthewConceive (Bib.Locus.page 64)],
        tradition := Tradition.christianTypological,
        confidence := Confidence.consensus } }
```

<a id="isaianicSignsAreOrdinaryEventsCited"></a>
**`isaianicSignsAreOrdinaryEventsCited`**

`isaianicSignsAreOrdinaryEvents`. What the text says: Rhodea lists
non-supernatural signs "including elsewhere in Isaiah" (64), and Wegner a sign
as "a common, everyday occurrence that has significance because of what it
means, foretells, or predicts" (470). Rydelnik, as Postell reports him (474),
grants the first of them: Isaiah's children are the "signs and wonders" of 8:18.

```lean

    kind := PremiseKind.textual,
    source :=
      { primary := Reference.scripture Scripture.ordinaryIsaianicSigns,
        supporting :=
          [Reference.work rhodeaDidMatthewConceive (Bib.Locus.page 64),

```

<a id="signDatedByAChildsInfancyCited"></a>
**`signDatedByAChildsInfancyCited`**

`signDatedByAChildsInfancy`. What 7:16 says, and common ground about which
child is left open: Wegner reads it of the child of 7:14 (477), Rydelnik of
