## TestimonyArguments.BornOfAVirgin.Results — what does and does not follow

Every result about the strands, each tagged `@[headline]` and each followed by
`#print axioms` so its trust base is visible in the source. The results about
Wegner's objection — its validity, its circle, and the replies to it, the
fathers' sign argument among them — are in `Results.Wegner`.

Entailments are established with `establish`; refutations name a countermodel
and use `refute_with`. A countermodel here is the rival's reading written down
as a valuation, which is why each one is a named definition with a docstring
saying what position it encodes rather than an anonymous function.

Read `hinges_jointly_load_bearing` first. It is the result the four-strand
encoding exists to make possible.

#### Results

<a id="christian_establishes"></a>
**`christian_establishes`**

Given the scriptural premises, the conclusion follows.

```lean
theorem christian_establishes : Establishes christian
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="catholic_establishes"></a>
**`catholic_establishes`**

The Roman Catholic package establishes it too, unsurprisingly: it is the
scriptural package with a further strand bolted on.

```lean
theorem catholic_establishes : Establishes catholic
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="magisterialOnly_establishes"></a>
**`magisterialOnly_establishes`**

The magisterial route carries the conclusion on its own, for a reader who
grants the authority it claims.

```lean
theorem magisterialOnly_establishes : Establishes magisterialOnly
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="criticalReading"></a>
**`criticalReading`**

The critical reading, written down: עַלְמָה means "young woman", Isaiah's
sign was given to Ahaz, Genesis 3:15 is an etiology, and Micah's silence about a
father is only silence. No virgin-birth criterion arises.

```lean
def criticalReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.almahMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.isaiahPredictsVirginBirth => False
    | Claim.genesis3_15IsProtoevangelium => False
    | Claim.seedOfTheWomanImpliesNoHumanFather => False
    | Claim.maternalSilenceImpliesNoHumanFather => False
    | Claim.messiahBornOfVirgin => False
    | Claim.jesusSatisfiesCriterion => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="critical_not_establishes"></a>
**`critical_not_establishes`**

The critical reading does not establish the conclusion.

```lean
theorem critical_not_establishes : ¬Establishes critical
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="criticalDenial_establishes"></a>
**`criticalDenial_establishes`**

The critical case for the denial does go through on its own terms. Stating
it as an argument rather than a bare assumption is what makes the next result
possible.

```lean
theorem criticalDenial_establishes : Establishes criticalDenial
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="berryReading"></a>
**`berryReading`**

Berry's reading, written down: the sign was given to Ahaz, how it was
fulfilled in his day is unclear, and so the near-term reading does not exclude
a further referent — leaving the predictive reading standing.

```lean
def berryReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.nearTermExcludesMessianicSense => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="berry_blocks_critical_denial"></a>
**`berry_blocks_critical_denial`**

**Berry's objection blocks the critical denial.** Grant that Isaiah 7:14
was a sign to Ahaz, and grant with Berry that how it was fulfilled in Ahaz's own
day is an open question, and the denial no longer follows.

This is the narrow thing the objection does, and it is worth being clear about
what it does not do. It does not establish the predictive reading, and it does
not touch the lexical dispute. It removes one route to the denial — the route
that runs through the near-term fulfilment — and leaves the argument where
`hinges_jointly_load_bearing` puts it.

```lean
theorem berry_blocks_critical_denial : ¬Establishes criticalDenialUnderBerry
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="parityReading"></a>
**`parityReading`**

The parity reading, written down: a near-term Assyrian setting is simply not
the kind of reason that rules out messianic reference, since Isaiah 9 and 11 sit
on that same timeline and are read messianically anyway.

```lean
def parityReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.nearTermExcludesMessianicSense => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="parity_blocks_critical_denial"></a>
**`parity_blocks_critical_denial`**

**Postell's parity argument blocks the critical denial too**, and by a
different route from Berry's.

Berry's objection is evidential — we do not know how the sign was fulfilled in
Ahaz's day. Parity is structural — the near-term setting was never the right
kind of reason, because Isaiah 9:5–6 and 11:1–10 stand on the same Assyrian
timeline and are read messianically without embarrassment. An opponent who
answers Berry by settling the near-term referent has not touched this.

```lean
theorem parity_blocks_critical_denial : ¬Establishes criticalDenialUnderParity
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="reformedReading"></a>
**`reformedReading`**

The Reformed objection, written down: papal teaching says what it says, and
saying it settles nothing, because Scripture is the supreme judge.

```lean
def reformedReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.magisteriumIsDoctrinallyAuthoritative => False
    | Claim.messiahBornOfVirgin => False
    | Claim.jesusSatisfiesCriterion => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="magisterial_authority_is_load_bearing"></a>
**`magisterial_authority_is_load_bearing`**

**What the magisterial strand is worth to a reader who does not grant the
magisterium's authority: nothing.** Deny that premise and the route collapses
outright, however firmly the teaching itself is attested.

This is why `christian` excludes it. A reader who holds with Westminster I.x
that Scripture is the supreme judge of controversies loses the whole of
`magisterialOnly` and must get the criterion from the four scriptural strands
or not at all.

```lean
theorem magisterial_authority_is_load_bearing : ¬Establishes magisterialDenied
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="almah_not_load_bearing"></a>
**`almah_not_load_bearing`**

**The lexical premise no longer carries the argument.** Strip `almah` and
the protoevangelium and Michean strands still deliver the criterion.

Before Genesis 3:15 and Micah 5:2–3 were encoded, this module proved the
opposite — and `almah_is_load_bearing_alone` below shows that the earlier
finding was right about the Isaianic strand taken by itself. What changed is
not the Isaianic evidence but the number of strands.

```lean
theorem almah_not_load_bearing : Establishes christianWithoutAlmah
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="withoutAlmahReading"></a>
**`withoutAlmahReading`**

A reading that grants everything in the Isaianic strand except the lexical
premise.

```lean
def withoutAlmahReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.almahMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.messiahBornOfVirgin => False
    | Claim.jesusSatisfiesCriterion => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="almah_is_load_bearing_alone"></a>
**`almah_is_load_bearing_alone`**

Within the Isaianic strand taken alone, the lexical premise is still
load-bearing: remove it and that strand yields nothing. The earlier
single-stranded encoding of this module is preserved here rather than deleted,
because it is what makes `almah_not_load_bearing` informative — the Isaianic
evidence did not get stronger, it got company.

```lean
theorem almah_is_load_bearing_alone : ¬Establishes isaianicStrandWithoutAlmah
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="admissibility_is_not_enough"></a>
**`admissibility_is_not_enough`**

**Admissibility is not enough.** Berry's lexical point is defensive — the
semantic range of עַלְמָה does not *exclude* the sense "virgin" — and defensive
is all it is. Substitute it for `almahMeansVirgin` and the Isaianic strand
yields nothing, on the same reading that refutes the strand without any lexical
premise at all.

The gap between *may mean* and *does mean* is where this argument lives, and
Berry is useful against the critical denial without narrowing it.

```lean
theorem admissibility_is_not_enough : ¬Establishes
    isaianicStrandOnAdmissibility
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

##### The referential strand

<a id="semantic_establishes"></a>
**`semantic_establishes`**

**The referential argument goes through.** Granted only what both sides
grant about the word — that עַלְמָה denotes a young woman of marriageable age,
and that being a virgin does not exclude a woman from that denotation — and
granted that Mary was such a woman and conceived as a virgin, Matthew's claim
turns out not to have required the lexical sense at all.

Nothing here asserts that עַלְמָה *means* virgin. The argument is about
reference, not sense, and it is cheaper for exactly that reason.

```lean
theorem semantic_establishes : Establishes semantic
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="lexicalCritical_establishes"></a>
**`lexicalCritical_establishes`**

The lexical objection, written down and granted its own premises.

```lean
theorem lexicalCritical_establishes : Establishes lexicalCritical
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="compatibilityReading"></a>
**`compatibilityReading`**

The referential reading, written down: the versions differ about which term
to use and not about who is described, so the divergence settles nothing about
the sense, and Matthew's claim never needed the sense.

```lean
def compatibilityReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.versionalDivergenceRefutesVirginSense => False
    | Claim.lexicalSenseRequiredForFulfilment => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="compatibility_defeats_lexical_objection"></a>
**`compatibility_defeats_lexical_objection`**

**The referential reply defeats the lexical objection.** Keep every
versional datum — the Targum's עוּלֵימְתָא, the Three's νεᾶνις, the Septuagint's
παρθένος, the Peshitta's ܒܬܘܠܬܐ, Qumran's confirmation of the Hebrew — add the
referential premises, and the objection no longer reaches its conclusion.

The tension in the versions is not evidence against the reading once virginity
is compatible with the word. It is evidence that four translators made four
defensible choices about how much of the referent's description to make
explicit.

```lean
theorem compatibility_defeats_lexical_objection : ¬Establishes
    lexicalCriticalUnderCompatibility
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="compatibilityOnlyReading"></a>
**`compatibilityOnlyReading`**

A reading on which Mary fits Isaiah's description and no criterion arises
from it.

```lean
def compatibilityOnlyReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.lexicalSenseRequiredForFulfilment => False
    | Claim.messiahBornOfVirgin => False
    | Claim.jesusSatisfiesCriterion => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="compatibility_does_not_establish_criterion"></a>
**`compatibility_does_not_establish_criterion`**

**What the referential argument costs.** It is purely defensive. It defeats
the objection without establishing the criterion: ask the same premises for
`jesusSatisfiesCriterion` and they do not deliver it, because nothing in them
says the Messiah *must* be born of a virgin — only that Mary may be described
as Isaiah describes.

This is the honest price of the move, and it is worth paying. The criterion has
to come from the Isaianic, protoevangelium or Michean strands; what the
referential argument buys is that losing the lexical dispute no longer costs
the fulfilment claim. Winning `almahMeansVirgin` outright was never necessary,
and this says so in a form either side can check.

```lean
theorem compatibility_does_not_establish_criterion : ¬Establishes
    semanticReachingForCriterion
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="noHingeReading"></a>
**`noHingeReading`**

A reading on which none of the four interpretive hinges holds: *almah*
means "young woman", the matrilineal wording of Genesis 3:15 implies nothing
about a father, Micah's silence is only silence, and Isaiah's composition does
not govern the sense of 7:14. Every textual observation is granted.

```lean
def noHingeReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.almahMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.seedOfTheWomanImpliesNoHumanFather => False
    | Claim.maternalSilenceImpliesNoHumanFather => False
    | Claim.compositionGovernsMeaning => False
    | Claim.messiahBornOfVirgin => False
    | Claim.jesusSatisfiesCriterion => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="hinges_jointly_load_bearing"></a>
**`hinges_jointly_load_bearing`**

**The result worth having.** No single hinge carries the argument, but the
four of them jointly do: remove all four and the criterion no longer follows,
with every textual and historical premise retained.

So the argument no longer hangs on the sense of עַלְמָה alone. It hangs on that
*or* on the matrilineal wording of Genesis 3:15 *or* on Micah's maternal
silence *or* on Postell's compositional reading — and an opponent must defeat
all four. That is a materially stronger position than the single-stranded
version, and a materially weaker one than four independent arguments would be:
three of the four hinges are `disputed` for good reason, and the module doc
says why.

```lean
theorem hinges_jointly_load_bearing : ¬Establishes christianWithoutAnyHinge
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="jesus_satisfies_virgin_birth"></a>
**`jesus_satisfies_virgin_birth`**

End to end: under the scriptural package, Jesus satisfies the virgin-birth
criterion.

```lean
theorem jesus_satisfies_virgin_birth : Satisfies jesus bornOfAVirgin
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### Satisfiability

`Entails` is vacuously true over a premise set with no model, so a package built
from contradictory premises would establish its conclusion with every gate
passing. Only packages carrying a positive `Establishes` result need checking:
one with a `¬ Establishes` result is satisfiable already, its countermodel being
a valuation on which every premise holds.

Several packages here *deny* a premise, so the all-holds reading will not serve
them — a model has to be the position's own world, which is the same discipline
the countermodels follow.

Not tagged `@[headline]`: these are claims about the health of the encoding.

<a id="everythingHoldsReading"></a>
**`everythingHoldsReading`**

The reading on which every claim holds at once.

```lean
def everythingHoldsReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun x => True
```

<a id="christian_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`christian_is_satisfiable`**

The scriptural package has a model.

```lean
theorem christian_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable christian.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="catholic_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`catholic_is_satisfiable`**

The Roman Catholic package has a model.

```lean
theorem catholic_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable catholic.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="magisterialOnly_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`magisterialOnly_is_satisfiable`**

The magisterial route has a model.

```lean
theorem magisterialOnly_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable magisterialOnly.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="christianWithoutAlmah_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`christianWithoutAlmah_is_satisfiable`**

The scriptural package minus the lexical premise has a model, so
`almah_not_load_bearing` is not vacuous.

```lean
theorem christianWithoutAlmah_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    christianWithoutAlmah.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="criticalDenialOwnReading"></a>
**`criticalDenialOwnReading`**

The critical denial's own world: the sign was Ahaz's, so Isaiah 7:14 is not
a prediction of a virgin birth.

```lean
def criticalDenialOwnReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.isaiahPredictsVirginBirth => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="criticalDenial_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`criticalDenial_is_satisfiable`**

The critical denial has a model.

```lean

-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="referentialOwnReading"></a>
**`referentialOwnReading`**

The referential argument's own world: Mary answers Isaiah's description, so
the fulfilment claim never required the lexical sense.

```lean
def referentialOwnReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.lexicalSenseRequiredForFulfilment => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="semantic_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`semantic_is_satisfiable`**

The referential argument has a model.

```lean
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="lexicalObjectionOwnReading"></a>

The lexical objection's own world: the versions read the broad term, so

```lean
    | Claim.jesusSatisfiesCriterion => False
```

## TestimonyArguments.BornOfAVirgin.Results.Wegner — Wegner's objection, and the sign

What follows from Wegner's grammatical objection and from the replies to it:
that it is valid, where its weight rests, the circle in it, Postell's usage
parity, and the fathers' sign argument together with the near-term reply to
that. `Dispute.Wegner` then asks who prevails when these meet.

Every result is tagged `@[headline]` and followed by `#print axioms`, as in
`Results.lean`, and every countermodel is a named reading.

#### Wegner's objection, and the circle in it

<a id="wegner_establishes"></a>
**`wegner_establishes`**

**Wegner's objection is valid on its own terms.** Grant the
predicate-adjective parse, grant that the pregnancy it reports is an ordinary
one, and grant that the one clear Isaianic referent settles what the word
denotes, and the lexical conclusion follows.

Stated first, and at full strength, because the results below are about where
its weight rests and are worth nothing if the argument was weak to begin
with.

```lean
theorem wegner_establishes : Establishes wegnerLexical
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="rydelnikReading"></a>
**`rydelnikReading`**

Rydelnik's reading, written down: הָרָה is the predicate adjective Wegner
says it is, and what it announces is the miracle rather than an ordinary
conception — the virgin is pregnant, a sign as deep as Sheol.

```lean
def rydelnikReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.pregnancyAtTheSignIsOrdinary => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsNotAVirgin => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="wegner_needs_ordinary_pregnancy"></a>
**`wegner_needs_ordinary_pregnancy`**

**The grammar is not what carries the objection.** Derive the ordinary
pregnancy the way Wegner derives it — from the near-term reading of the sign —
rather than granting it, and the argument no longer reaches its conclusion,
with the parse itself untouched.

So the load-bearing premise is not `harahIsPredicateAdjective`, which both
sides grant, but the reading of the sign that makes the pregnancy an ordinary
one. The next result follows that premise back to where it comes from.

```lean
theorem wegner_needs_ordinary_pregnancy : ¬Establishes
    wegnerWithoutOrdinaryPregnancy
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="wegnerConclusionGrantedReading"></a>
**`wegnerConclusionGrantedReading`**

Wegner's own conclusion granted: עַלְמָה does not denote a virgin, and
Isaiah 7:14 is not a prediction of a virgin birth. The same two legs of the
circle are satisfied on this reading as on the one below — the first because
its antecedent fails, the second because its consequent holds — which is what
makes the circle silent in *both* directions rather than merely unhelpful in
one.

Not a convenience: it is the position Wegner argues for, and the reading had to
be found rather than assumed. The all-true valuation that serves the same
purpose in `SolaScriptura` does not work here, because `wegnerCircle` carries
negated grounds.

```lean
def wegnerConclusionGrantedReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.almahMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.isaiahPredictsVirginBirth => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="circleUngroundedReading"></a>
**`circleUngroundedReading`**

The reading that exhibits the circle: the predictive reading of Isaiah 7:14
stands, עַלְמָה may denote a virgin, and the pregnancy the sign announces is not
an ordinary one. Every uncontested datum in Wegner's case is granted — the
parse, the near-term setting, the referent principle — and the two legs of the
circle are satisfied because each is an implication whose antecedent fails.

```lean
def circleUngroundedReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.pregnancyAtTheSignIsOrdinary => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsNotAVirgin => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="circle_leaves_the_lexical_conclusion_open"></a>
**`circle_leaves_the_lexical_conclusion_open`**

**The circle, shown rather than alleged.** Put both legs in place — the
reading supplying the ordinary pregnancy, and the lexical conclusion turned
back against the reading — keep every uncontested datum, and the lexical
conclusion does not follow.

`circleUngroundedReading` is why: a cycle of implications is satisfied outright
by a valuation on which every node in it is false, because each leg then has a
false antecedent. Nothing enters such a loop from outside, so nothing comes out
of it. That is what it means for an argument to be circular rather than sound,
and it is checkable rather than merely assertable.

What this does **not** show is that Wegner is wrong. `wegner_establishes`
records that his argument is valid; what the circle costs is the claim that it
is an *independent* route to the lexical conclusion. And the result is
conditional on `readingSuppliesOrdinaryPregnancy`, which is Postell's reading
of Wegner's procedure, not Wegner's own account of it. He would say the
near-term reading rests on the historical setting and stands without the
lexical finding — in which case the premise is false and the circle is not
there. That premise is where a defender of Wegner should press.

```lean
theorem circle_leaves_the_lexical_conclusion_open : Independent
    wegnerCircle.premises (notP Claim.almahMeansVirgin)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="circle_leaves_the_denial_open"></a>
**`circle_leaves_the_denial_open`**

**And the other end of it is no better off.** The same premises, asked for
the denial of the predictive reading instead of the lexical conclusion, fail in
the same way and on the same reading.

Both results are needed to make the point. A circle is not an argument that
fails to establish one of its nodes; it is one that establishes neither, having
no premise outside itself.

```lean
theorem circle_leaves_the_denial_open : Independent wegnerCircle.premises
    (notP Claim.isaiahPredictsVirginBirth)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="usageParityReading"></a>
**`usageParityReading`**

Postell's usage reading, written down: the עַלְמָה of Isaiah 7:14 is granted
to be no virgin, and a single referent still does not settle what the word
denotes — because the other clear cases would settle it the other way.

```lean
def usageParityReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.oneReferentSettlesDenotation => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="usage_parity_blocks_wegner"></a>
**`usage_parity_blocks_wegner`**

**Postell's second reply, and it is independent of the first.** Concede the
parse, concede the ordinary pregnancy, concede that the woman of Isaiah 7:14 is
no virgin — and the lexical conclusion still does not follow, because the
principle that carries it there would carry the other clear cases the opposite
way.

This one survives the defence suggested above. An opponent who shows that the
near-term reading stands on its own, and so that there is no circle, has not
touched the usage parity: the method is still selective. Between them the two
replies leave the objection needing both a non-circular route to the ordinary
pregnancy and a reason to privilege this occurrence over Genesis 24:43.

```lean
theorem usage_parity_blocks_wegner : ¬Establishes wegnerUnderUsageParity
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### The fathers' sign argument

Justin, Irenaeus and Origen answer the near-term reading with one argument. The
oracle promised a *sign*, one offered "in the depth or in the height" (7:11),
and an ordinary conception happens to every woman who is not barren. So the
pregnancy of 7:14 is not an ordinary one, and that is the ground of Wegner's
objection that the grammar does not supply.

The near-term reply is that a sign need not be a miracle. Isaiah's own children
are "signs and portents" (8:18), and this sign is dated by a child's infancy
(7:16), so its point may be its timing.

<a id="referentialSignReading"></a>
**`referentialSignReading`**

The fathers' sign, with the word left to the lexicon: the pregnancy of 7:14
is no ordinary one, and עַלְמָה still does not denote a virgin. It is the
referential reading's world, in which Mary is an עַלְמָה without the word
carrying the sense. Every premise of Wegner's objection under the sign argument
holds in it, and so does his lexical conclusion.

```lean
def referentialSignReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.almahMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.pregnancyAtTheSignIsOrdinary => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsNotAVirgin => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="sign_leaves_the_lexical_conclusion_open"></a>
**`sign_leaves_the_lexical_conclusion_open`**

**The sign argument blocks Wegner's objection, and settles nothing about
the word.** Keep the parse, the near-term setting and the referent principle,
put the fathers' two grounds where the ordinary pregnancy was, and the lexical
conclusion is independent of what is left. On Rydelnik's reading it fails: the
virgin is pregnant, a sign as deep as Sheol. On `referentialSignReading` it
holds.

So the argument answers the objection where `wegner_needs_ordinary_pregnancy`
says its weight rests, and does no more. It does not show that עַלְמָה denotes a
virgin, because it is not about the word at all.

```lean
theorem sign_leaves_the_lexical_conclusion_open : Independent
    wegnerUnderTheSign.premises (notP Claim.almahMeansVirgin)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="nearTermSignReading"></a>
**`nearTermSignReading`**

The near-term reading of the sign, in Wegner's world: a sign need not be a
miracle, the pregnancy is an ordinary one, עַלְמָה does not denote a virgin, and
nor, in the Septuagint's day, did παρθένος.

```lean
def nearTermSignReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.maternalSilenceImpliesNoHumanFather => False
    | Claim.magisteriumIsDoctrinallyAuthoritative => False
    | Claim.signMustBeExtraordinary => False
    | Claim.almahMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.parthenosMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.lawsUseParthenosAsVirgin => False
    | Claim.dinahIsTheLawsParthenos => False
    | Claim.lxxIsaiahUsesParthenosAsVirgin => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="marvelAnywayReading"></a>
**`marvelAnywayReading`**

A sign that need not be a marvel, and is one all the same: the reader who
grants the near-term reply and still holds that the pregnancy of 7:14 is no
ordinary one, on other grounds than the sign.

```lean
def marvelAnywayReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.signMustBeExtraordinary => False
    | Claim.pregnancyAtTheSignIsOrdinary => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="reply_leaves_the_pregnancy_open"></a>
**`reply_leaves_the_pregnancy_open`**

**The near-term reply blocks the sign argument back, and settles nothing
about the pregnancy.** Put the reply's grounds and step where the fathers' first
ground was, keep the second, and whether the pregnancy is an ordinary one is
independent of what is left: it is on `nearTermSignReading` and it is not on
`marvelAnywayReading`.

This is the reply's whole reach. It takes away the fathers' reason for denying
the ordinary pregnancy; it does not supply Wegner's reason for asserting it,
which still comes from the near-term reading of the sign.

```lean
theorem reply_leaves_the_pregnancy_open : Independent
    signArgumentUnderReply.premises (notP Claim.pregnancyAtTheSignIsOrdinary)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### Satisfiability

As in `Results.lean`: only a package with a positive `Establishes` result needs
a model named, and the sign argument and the reply are given theirs in
`Dispute.Wegner`, where they are established.

<a id="wegnerOwnReading"></a>
**`wegnerOwnReading`**

Wegner's own world: the one clear Isaianic referent is not a virgin, so the
word does not denote virginity.

```lean
def wegnerOwnReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.almahMeansVirgin => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="wegnerLexical_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`wegnerLexical_is_satisfiable`**

Wegner's objection has a model.

```lean
theorem wegnerLexical_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable wegnerLexical.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

## TestimonyArguments.BornOfAVirgin.Results.Septuagint — what the Septuagint shows

A reader's question, in a reader's words: *the Jews who translated Isaiah into
Greek, before Christ, wrote παρθένος — "virgin". Doesn't that settle it?*

The argument is old. Irenaeus makes it against Theodotion and Aquila: the verse
"was interpreted into Greek by the Jews themselves, much before the period of
our Lord's advent, that there might remain no suspicion that perchance the Jews,
complying with our humour, did put this interpretation upon these words"
(*Against Heresies* III.21.1). This module encodes it at full strength and asks
three things of it, one result each.

**What it rests on.** Take away the claim that παρθένος, in the translator's
Greek, means a virgin, and the Septuagint no longer shows that its translator
read the woman as one (`parthenos_is_load_bearing`). Everything turns on that
word, and whether it means "virgin" there is exactly what the sources dispute.
Rico and Gentry hold that it does "whenever it appears in Semitic Koine Greek",
and Bratcher agrees. Wegner, Rhodea and Meade hold that in the translator's day
it still meant a young woman, as it does of Dinah after Shechem has lain with her
(Genesis 34:3), and Walton that the translator's choice of it "is not
necessarily betraying an interpretation as virgin". Wegner and Walton grant that
by the New Testament the word meant "virgin"; Meade and Davidson put that sense
down to Christian use. The dispute is over the translator's day, two or three
centuries before Matthew. The Greek Pentateuch's laws use the word where
virginity is the point, and its law of the seduced παρθένος reads Genesis 34:3
itself otherwise: the woman a man has lain with is still the law's παρθένος, and
owed "the bride-price of virgins" (Exodus 22:15–16). `Dispute.Septuagint` weighs
all five, and the Septuagint's witness prevails, with Rico and Gentry, the laws
and that reading of Genesis 34:3; Wegner cannot be defended
(`septuagint_prevails_over_wegner`). The verdict turns on one rating, the
status reading's step, `plausible` on the readers found.

**What it would show, if the word means "virgin".** How one early reader read
Isaiah: a Jewish translator, before Christ, read the woman of 7:14 as a virgin, so
reading her so is no Christian invention. It would not show what Isaiah's own word
means without a further step, rated `disputed`
(`septuagint_word_rests_on_its_inference`). A translator can render the woman
described rather than the word. The translator of Genesis wrote παρθένος for the
עַלְמָה Rebekah (24:43), whom the story has already called a virgin (24:16): a
rendering "historically correct — since Rebekah was a virgin", Bratcher says,
that "does not precisely translate the Hebrew" (113). Elsewhere the Septuagint's
translators, of other books than Isaiah, render עַלְמָה with νεᾶνις, "young
woman", four times. That is how this argument's referential strand already reads
the versions.

**What it leaves open, even then.** The Greek says the virgin *shall* be with
child. A woman who is a virgin when the sign is given and conceives later by a
man fits those words as well as a virgin who conceives as a virgin does
(`septuagint_leaves_the_conception_open`). That is not only a rival's reading.
Bratcher, who holds that παρθένος "definitely means 'virgin' in the LXX" (113),
reads the Greek of 7:14 so: "a young woman, at that time virgin, would in the
normal way marry and bear a child" (115), "the most reasonable explanation"
(116). So the Septuagint, granted every word, does not by itself say that the
conception was without a man. Justin and
Irenaeus read it so, from the promise of a sign (`signLine`, weighed in
`Dispute.Wegner`); the word alone does not.

#### The Septuagint as a witness

Each reading below is a model: a way every claim of the argument could stand at
once, named for what it says of the Septuagint and of the woman of 7:14. It
settles those as its namesake does. Where the argument's joins require a side on
questions this module does not touch, it takes the scriptural reading's: that
Micah's mention of a mother and no father does mean something, and that
Scripture, not the magisterium, is the judge. Every other claim it leaves true,
and none of them bears on the results it is used for.

<a id="virginConceivesReading"></a>
**`virginConceivesReading`**

Justin's reading of the elders' Greek, with Rico and Gentry's sense of the
word: παρθένος means a virgin, the translator read the woman of 7:14 as one, and
she conceives as one — "a sign which is not common to all the first-born sons"
(*Dialogue* 84). So she is not already pregnant when the sign is given, and her
pregnancy is no ordinary one. Wegner's claim is false in it: the word already
had the sense "virgin".

```lean
def virginConceivesReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.parthenosMeantYoungWoman => False
    | Claim.harahIsPredicateAdjective => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsAlreadyPregnant => False
    | Claim.pregnancyAtTheSignIsOrdinary => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsNotAVirgin => False
    | Claim.maternalSilenceProvesNothing => False
    | Claim.magisteriumIsDoctrinallyAuthoritative => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="septuagintWitness_establishes"></a>
**`septuagintWitness_establishes`**

**The Septuagint, read with Rico and Gentry, is a witness from before
Christ.** Grant that the Greek Isaiah renders עַלְמָה with παρθένος, that it was
made by Jews before Christ, and that παρθένος in its Greek means a virgin, and
it follows that a Jewish translator, before Christ, read the woman of 7:14 as a
virgin.

That is the whole of what it delivers: a claim about how the first translator
read the verse. It does not show that παρθένος meant "virgin" in the
translator's day: that is granted here, and rated `disputed`
(`parthenos_is_load_bearing`). Nor does it show what עַלְמָה means
(`septuagint_word_rests_on_its_inference`), or how the woman conceived
(`septuagint_leaves_the_conception_open`).

```lean
theorem septuagintWitness_establishes : Establishes septuagintWitness
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="septuagintWitness_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`septuagintWitness_is_satisfiable`**

The Septuagint as a witness has a model.

```lean
theorem septuagintWitness_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    septuagintWitness.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="wegnerDriftReading"></a>
**`wegnerDriftReading`**

Wegner's reading: in the translator's day παρθένος meant "young woman", with
or without virginity, and did not yet mean "virgin"; so the Greek does not show
that its translator read the woman of 7:14 as a virgin, nor anything about how
she conceived, and עַלְמָה does not denote a virgin either. The woman of 7:14 is
already pregnant when the sign is given, and the sign need not be a miracle.
Wegner does not take up the laws of the Greek Pentateuch. This reading extends
his view to them as Miller reads them: the laws say what they say, and the word
in them still means "young woman". Nor does he take up Exodus 22:15–16; in this
reading Genesis 34 is told in that law's words, and Dinah is still called a
παρθένος in the older sense.

```lean
def wegnerDriftReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.parthenosMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.lawsUseParthenosAsVirgin => False
    | Claim.dinahIsTheLawsParthenos => False
    | Claim.lxxIsaiahUsesParthenosAsVirgin => False
    | Claim.lxxReadsAVirgin => False
    | Claim.lxxEnvisagesAVirginalConception => False
    | Claim.almahMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.signMustBeExtraordinary => False
    | Claim.maternalSilenceProvesNothing => False
    | Claim.magisteriumIsDoctrinallyAuthoritative => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="parthenos_is_load_bearing"></a>
**`parthenos_is_load_bearing`**

**The word carries the whole witness.** Keep the rendering and its date —
the Greek has παρθένος, and Jews made it before Christ — and grant nothing about
what παρθένος meant to them, and the Septuagint no longer shows that its
translator read the woman as a virgin. On Wegner's reading the word was the
ordinary one for a young woman of marriageable age.

So whoever argues from the Septuagint has to win the claim about the word. Its
date, which the rival grants, does not help without it.

```lean
theorem parthenos_is_load_bearing : ¬Establishes septuagintWithoutTheSense
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### From the translator's reading to Isaiah's word

<a id="septuagintOnTheWord_establishes"></a>
**`septuagintOnTheWord_establishes`**

Add the step from the translator's reading to Isaiah's word, rated
`disputed`, and the case concludes that עַלְמָה denotes a virgin. It is only as
good as that step.

```lean
theorem septuagintOnTheWord_establishes : Establishes septuagintOnTheWord
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="septuagintOnTheWord_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`septuagintOnTheWord_is_satisfiable`**

The Septuagint asked for Isaiah's word has a model.

```lean
theorem septuagintOnTheWord_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    septuagintOnTheWord.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="translatorDescribesTheWomanReading"></a>
**`translatorDescribesTheWomanReading`**

The referential reading of the Septuagint: its translator read the woman of
7:14 as a virgin, with a word that means one, and עַלְמָה still denotes only a
young woman of marriageable age. He described the woman, not the word, and the
woman is a virgin.

```lean
def translatorDescribesTheWomanReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.parthenosMeantYoungWoman => False
    | Claim.almahMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.harahIsPredicateAdjective => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsAlreadyPregnant => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsNotAVirgin => False
    | Claim.maternalSilenceProvesNothing => False
    | Claim.magisteriumIsDoctrinallyAuthoritative => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="septuagint_word_rests_on_its_inference"></a>
**`septuagint_word_rests_on_its_inference`**

**The Septuagint shows how its translator read the woman, not what Isaiah's
word means.** Grant everything the witness rests on, παρθένος as "virgin"
included, and grant that the translator read the woman of 7:14 as a virgin:
עַלְמָה can still denote only a young woman, as the referential strand reads it.
The step from the one to the other is the weight, and it is rated `disputed`:
Bratcher and Brown grant that the translator read the woman as a virgin and deny
that עַלְמָה says so, and Walton holds that the Greek shows "at best ... an
interpretational preference rather than a linguistic necessity" (293). On
Bratcher's reading (113), the Septuagint's translators render the woman, not the
word: παρθένος for Rebekah, whom the story calls a virgin (Genesis 24:43), and
νεᾶνις at Exodus 2:8, Psalm 67:26 (68:25 in English Bibles), Song 1:3 and 6:8.
Jerome reads Rebekah the other way, as showing that עַלְמָה denotes a virgin
(*Against Jovinianus* I.32).

So the Septuagint cannot by itself settle the claim that עַלְמָה itself denotes a
virgin, however its word is read. If its word means "virgin", what it can do is
what the referential strand already needs: show that a virgin answers the
description.

```lean
theorem septuagint_word_rests_on_its_inference : ¬Entails
    septuagintLine.premises (p Claim.almahMeansVirgin)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### What the Greek leaves open

<a id="nowAVirginReading"></a>
**`nowAVirginReading`**

Bratcher's reading of the Greek, who holds that its word means a virgin: "a
young woman, at that time virgin, would in the normal way marry and bear a
child" (115). Rhodea gives the Greek the same reading, granting its sense for
argument's sake and quoting Tsevat: "The pregnancy lies in the future ...;
nothing indicates that the woman is also a virgin after the conception" (67).
The word means a virgin, the translator read her as one, and she is one when the
sign is given; she conceives later, by a man.

```lean
def nowAVirginReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.parthenosMeantYoungWoman => False
    | Claim.lxxEnvisagesAVirginalConception => False
    | Claim.harahIsPredicateAdjective => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsAlreadyPregnant => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsNotAVirgin => False
    | Claim.maternalSilenceProvesNothing => False
    | Claim.magisteriumIsDoctrinallyAuthoritative => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="septuagint_leaves_the_conception_open"></a>
**`septuagint_leaves_the_conception_open`**

**Granted every word, the Septuagint leaves the conception open.** Keep the
rendering, its date, παρθένος as "virgin", the reading it delivers, and the tense
of the verb — the virgin *shall* be with child — and whether its translator
meant a conception without a man is independent of all of it. On Bratcher's
reading, who holds that the word means a virgin, she is a virgin when the sign is
given and later conceives in the ordinary way; Rhodea reads it so too, granting
the sense for argument's sake. On Justin's she conceives as a virgin. Both
readings keep every premise.

No premise here speaks to how she conceives, so the result says only that the
Greek's own words leave it open. Justin's argument that an ordinary conception
would be no sign is the sign argument's, and is weighed in `Dispute.Wegner`.

The result has two halves: the Greek does not show that the translator meant a
conception without a man, and does not show that he did not. If its sense is
granted, the Septuagint's word answers the objection that the virgin reading was
a Christian invention; it does not supply the virginal conception. That comes, if
it comes, from the promise of a sign (`signLine`), or from Matthew and Luke.

```lean
theorem septuagint_leaves_the_conception_open : Independent
    septuagintWithTheFuture.premises (p Claim.lxxEnvisagesAVirginalConception)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

## TestimonyArguments.BornOfAVirgin.Results.Genesis — what "her seed" says of a father

A reader's question, in a reader's words: *Genesis 3:15 promises that "her seed"
will strike the serpent's head — the woman's seed, not the man's. Doesn't that
already point to a virgin conception? And doesn't the Greek, which calls the
seed "he", make it plainer?*

The short answer: it may, but the text does not settle it. Whether naming the
seed as the woman's *says* there will be no human father is a live dispute among
readers most of whom hold the virgin birth, and the library finds it a tie
(`nothing_prevails_over_her_seed`, in `Dispute.Genesis`). That the wording
*fits* the virgin birth, once it has happened, Luther's side and Leupold and
Keil all grant. The Greek may show
that its translator expected one person; it does not show how that person would
be born.

The protoevangelium strand of this argument holds, as a premise, that the seed
being named as the woman's marks a birth with no human father
(`seedOfTheWomanImpliesNoHumanFather`). "Marks" is vague on purpose, as its
holders leave it: Miravalle's own word is "hint". This module asks what it can
mean, and what each meaning can bear.

**Read as what the wording itself signifies**, it is Luther's argument: the seed
of other women "might rather be said to have been the seed of the man", but
Mary's was "the true Seed of Mary" (*Luther on the Creation* 298–99). He finds
the sense in the words of Genesis, and holds that Isaiah later "threw some
additional light" on it, so that "it was then made certain" (298).
`herSeedCase_establishes` grants him every ground and checks that the argument
goes through. It rests on his step (`her_seed_rests_on_its_inference`). The
Lutheran commentators Leupold and Keil, who hold the virgin birth, grant every
ground and deny the step. Leupold, asked whether the expression is "so phrased
in reference to Mary and the virgin birth", answers "Not primarily, but at least
incidentally": it "does not specifically prophesy the virgin birth" (169). Keil
finds the virgin birth in the promise's fulfilment, "even if the words had
reference first of all to the fact that the woman had been led astray" (102).
Jack P. Lewis denies the step too, pointing to Hagar and Rebekah, whose seed
Genesis also calls theirs (299–300); he doubts the promise reading itself, but
his argument does not need that doubt.

**Read as what the wording fits, once fulfilled**, it is granted by Leupold and
Keil, who deny the first reading. Leupold: "it coincides and agrees with it under
divine providence" (169). Keil: the promise was fulfilled "even in its apparently
casual form" (102). But they reach the fit from the conception: the wording is
seen to fit once the birth is known. Read this way, the verse confirms the
virgin birth to one who already believes it, and gives no reason to believe it
to one who does not. That is what the reading's own grounds say; it is not a
separate theorem. `whatHerSeedMarks` sets out both readings and what answers
each.

**The promise, and its fulfilment.** Whether the wording foretold a virgin birth
is one question. Whether the promise is fulfilled in Jesus is another, and it
does not need the first. Every term of the verse is met as the New Testament
names it: the woman's seed, the Son "made of a woman" (Galatians 4:4); the
serpent, "that old serpent, called the Devil" (Revelation 12:9); its head
crushed, when the Son destroys the devil "through death" (Hebrews 2:14); his heel
struck, in his death and rising. That fulfilment confirms that the verse was a
promise, and it does so for a reader who denies the virginal conception too.
With the virginal conception, it says one thing more: the seed in whom the
promise is fulfilled was of the woman alone. `Dispute.Protoevangelium` weighs
the fulfilment against Westermann's denial that the verse is a promise at
all.

**The Greek's "he".** The Septuagint calls the woman's seed "he", αὐτός, though
σπέρμα is neuter, and Collins finds it "beyond question that the translator of
Genesis 3:15 meant to convey that an individual was promised" (145)
(`greekHeCase_establishes`). If so, it shows how one Jewish translator before
Christ read the promise, and reading it of one person is no Christian invention.
But the earliest known reader of that Greek did not read it so: Philo calls the
masculine "as to its language, a barbarism, but, as to the meaning … a correct
expression", and takes "he" of the mind (*Allegorical Interpretation* III.188).
The claim is `disputed` on him. No other text before Christ reads the verse of
one victor; the Targums, later, read it of "the sons of the woman", with a
remedy "in the days of the King Messiah" (Lewis 301).
Whether the Hebrew says so is a further question: Collins argues that its syntax
is "quite consistent with the pattern where a single individual is in view"
(145), and reports that many think it does not (141); Lewis, who grants the
Greek's reading, allows that the masculine "could be an oversight" (300). Either
way,
the Greek says nothing of a father (`the_greek_he_leaves_the_father_open`): the
same Greek calls the seed Hannah asks for "him" (1 Samuel 1:11), and the seed
promised to David "he" (2 Samuel 7:12–14), and each has a father. Irenaeus,
quoting the verse as the Greek gives it, "He shall be on the watch for thy
head", reads it of "He who should be born of a woman, [namely] from the Virgin"
(*Against Heresies* V.21.1); but he does not argue from the pronoun to the
conception, and no reader found does.

`Dispute.Genesis` weighs Luther's case against Leupold's and Lewis's.

#### Two readings of the woman's seed

Each reading below is a model: one way every claim of the argument could be true
at once, named for what it says of the wording of Genesis 3:15. Some pairs of
claims in this argument cannot both be true, so each model has to take a side on
them; on questions this module does not touch it takes the scriptural reading's
side: that the Septuagint's παρθένος means a virgin, that Micah's mention of a
mother and no father does mean something, and that Scripture, not the
magisterium, is the judge. Every other claim it leaves true, and none of them
bears on the results it is used for.

<a id="lutherReading"></a>
**`lutherReading`**

Luther's reading: the seed named as the woman's, and not a man's, signifies
a birth with no human father, and the promise is fulfilled in one so born.

```lean
def lutherReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.parthenosMeantYoungWoman => False
    | Claim.maternalSilenceProvesNothing => False
    | Claim.magisteriumIsDoctrinallyAuthoritative => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="leupoldReading"></a>
**`leupoldReading`**

Leupold's reading: the promise is of the victor, "her seed" is first
collective, the woman's posterity, the woman is named because she was deceived,
and the wording does not itself signify a birth without a human father — though
it fits one, as fulfilled. Lewis's claims hold in it too: Genesis speaks of a
woman's seed in ordinary births. And "her seed", though collective first, is not
only a line of descendants: "the word is also used in reference to an individual"
(168).

```lean
def leupoldReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.wordingSignifiesAFatherlessBirth => False
    | Claim.seedIsLineNotIndividual => False
    | Claim.parthenosMeantYoungWoman => False
    | Claim.maternalSilenceProvesNothing => False
    | Claim.magisteriumIsDoctrinallyAuthoritative => False
    | x => True
```

#### The wording read as signifying

<a id="herSeedCase_establishes"></a>
**`herSeedCase_establishes`**

**Luther's case from the wording goes through.** Grant that Genesis 3:15
names the seed as the woman's, that it is the first promise of a redeemer, that
a man's seed is ordinarily reckoned through him, and Luther's step from these to
the wording's sense: the wording signifies a birth with no human father.

It does not show that the step is sound — Leupold, Keil and Lewis deny it
(`her_seed_rests_on_its_inference`) — nor that the promise was fulfilled.

```lean
theorem herSeedCase_establishes : Establishes herSeedCase
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="herSeedCase_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`herSeedCase_is_satisfiable`**

Luther's case has a model: his own reading.

```lean
theorem herSeedCase_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable herSeedCase.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="her_seed_rests_on_its_inference"></a>
**`her_seed_rests_on_its_inference`**

**The wording's sense rests on Luther's step.** Grant every ground — the
seed named as the woman's, Genesis 3:15 as the first promise of a redeemer, a
man's seed reckoned through him — and it still does not follow that the wording
signifies a birth with no human father. Leupold and Keil grant those grounds and
deny it, and Lewis, granting the messianic reading for argument's sake, denies
it too. On Leupold's reading the seed is named the woman's because she was
deceived, and "her seed" is first collective, her posterity.

So the claim does not follow from the grounds alone: it needs Luther's step,
rated `disputed`. That does not show the step is wrong, only that the wording,
which both sides read, does not decide between them.

```lean
theorem her_seed_rests_on_its_inference : ¬Entails herSeedLine.grounds (p
    Claim.wordingSignifiesAFatherlessBirth)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="posterityCase_establishes"></a>
**`posterityCase_establishes`**

Leupold's case goes through on its own grounds.

```lean
theorem posterityCase_establishes : Establishes posterityCase
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="posterityCase_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`posterityCase_is_satisfiable`**

Leupold's case has a model: his own reading.

```lean
theorem posterityCase_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable posterityCase.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="idiomCase_establishes"></a>
**`idiomCase_establishes`**

Lewis's case goes through on its own grounds.

```lean
theorem idiomCase_establishes : Establishes idiomCase
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="idiomCase_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`idiomCase_is_satisfiable`**

Lewis's case has a model: Leupold's reading, in which Lewis's claims hold
too.

```lean
theorem idiomCase_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable idiomCase.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### The Greek's "he"

<a id="greekHeCase_establishes"></a>
**`greekHeCase_establishes`**

**The Greek reads one person.** Grant that the Septuagint refers to the
woman's seed with the masculine αὐτός, though σπέρμα is neuter, and the step
Collins and Martin take from it, and its translator read the seed as one person.

That is all it delivers: who that person is, and how he is born, it does not
say.

```lean
theorem greekHeCase_establishes : Establishes greekHeCase
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="greekHeCase_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`greekHeCase_is_satisfiable`**

The Greek's line has a model.

```lean
theorem greekHeCase_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable greekHeCase.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="the_greek_he_leaves_the_father_open"></a>
**`the_greek_he_leaves_the_father_open`**

**The Greek's "he" leaves the father open.** Keep the Greek's masculine "he"
and the reading of one person drawn from it, and every ground of Luther's case
— the seed named as the woman's, the first promise of a redeemer, a man's seed
reckoned through him — and whether the wording signifies a birth with no human
father is independent of all of it. On Luther's reading it does; on Leupold's,
granted the Greek, it does not.

The result has two halves: the Greek does not show that the one person promised
has no human father, and does not show that he has one. The plain reason is in
the Greek itself: it calls the seed Hannah asks for "him" (1 Samuel 1:11), and
the seed promised to David "he" (2 Samuel 7:12–14), as Collins shows (144), and
each has a father. One person, called "he", can have a father. What the Greek
shows is how its translator read the promise: of one person. Collins argues
that the Hebrew's syntax is "quite consistent with the pattern where a single
individual is in view" (145); Leupold reaches one person at the promise's end,
and Keil reaches Christ "not as an individual, but as the head" of the woman's
posterity (102). No reader found argues that the Greek's "he" answers Lewis's
point from Hagar and Rebekah.

```lean
theorem the_greek_he_leaves_the_father_open : Independent
    greekHeWithThePromise.premises (p Claim.wordingSignifiesAFatherlessBirth)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### What "marks" means: the dilemma

<a id="asWhatTheWordingSignifies"></a>
**`asWhatTheWordingSignifies`**

The hinge **read as what the wording itself signifies**: Luther's reading,
and the one Miravalle and Henry give.

```lean
def asWhatTheWordingSignifies : Reading Claim :=
  { name := "as what the wording itself signifies",
    commits := p Claim.wordingSignifiesAFatherlessBirth,
    source :=
      { primary := Reference.work lutherOnTheCreation (Bib.Locus.pages 298 299),
        supporting :=
          [Reference.work miravalleMeetYourMother,
            Reference.work henryCommentary
              (Bib.Locus.adLoc Scripture.genesis3_15)],
        tradition := Tradition.christianTypological,
        confidence := Confidence.disputed } }
```

<a id="asWhatTheWordingFits"></a>
**`asWhatTheWordingFits`**

The hinge **read as what the wording fits, once fulfilled**: Leupold's and
Keil's reading, which rests the fit on the virginal conception itself.

```lean
def asWhatTheWordingFits : Reading Claim :=
  { name := "as what the wording fits, once fulfilled",
    commits := p Claim.wordingFitsAFatherlessBirth,
    grounds :=
      [p Claim.maryConceivedAsVirgin,
        p Claim.maryConceivedAsVirgin 🡒
          p Claim.wordingFitsAFatherlessBirth],
    source :=
      { primary := Reference.work leupoldGenesis (Bib.Locus.page 169),
        supporting :=
          [Reference.work keilDelitzschPentateuch (Bib.Locus.page 102)],
        tradition := Tradition.christianHistoricalGrammatical,
        confidence := Confidence.disputed } }
```

<a id="protoevangeliumAsSignifying"></a>
**`protoevangeliumAsSignifying`** — Protoevangelium strand (Genesis 3:15), read as what the wording itself signifies

The protoevangelium strand with its hinge read as Luther reads it.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(1)} \quad &amp; P_{50} \\
\text{(2)} \quad &amp; P_{51} \\
\text{(3)} \quad &amp; P_{52} \\
\text{(4)} \quad &amp; P_{53} \\
\text{(5)} \quad &amp; (P_{50} \land P_{51} \land P_{52} \land P_{53}) \rightarrow P_{90} \\
\text{(6)} \quad &amp; P_{53} \rightarrow P_{54} \\[4pt]
\vdash \quad &amp; P_{90}
\end{aligned}
\]
</div>

No premise here rests on scripture alone.

<a id="protoevangeliumAsFitting"></a>
**`protoevangeliumAsFitting`** — Protoevangelium strand (Genesis 3:15), read as what the wording fits, once fulfilled

The protoevangelium strand with its hinge read as Leupold reads it.

<div class="testimony-math">
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{(1)} \quad &amp; P_{50} \\
\text{(2)} \quad &amp; P_{51} \\
\text{(3)} \quad &amp; P_{52} \\
\text{(4)} \quad &amp; P_{53} \\
\text{(5)} \quad &amp; (P_{50} \land P_{51} \land P_{52} \land P_{53}) \rightarrow P_{90} \\
\text{(6)} \quad &amp; P_{76} \\
\text{(7)} \quad &amp; P_{76} \rightarrow P_{55} \\
\text{(8)} \quad &amp; P_{53} \rightarrow P_{55} \\[4pt]
\vdash \quad &amp; P_{90}
\end{aligned}
\]
</div>

No premise here rests on scripture alone.

<a id="protoevangeliumAsSignifying_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`protoevangeliumAsSignifying_is_satisfiable`**

**The strand, read as Luther reads its hinge, is consistent**: its premises
can all be true together, so any answer to it must come from outside it.

```lean
theorem protoevangeliumAsSignifying_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    protoevangeliumAsSignifying.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="protoevangeliumAsFitting_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`protoevangeliumAsFitting_is_satisfiable`**

**The strand, read as Leupold reads its hinge, is consistent** too.

```lean
theorem protoevangeliumAsFitting_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    protoevangeliumAsFitting.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="posterity_does_not_reach_the_fit"></a>
**`posterity_does_not_reach_the_fit`**

**Leupold has no quarrel with the second reading; he holds it.** Read as
what the wording fits once fulfilled, the strand's hinge can be held with every
premise of Leupold's case.

```lean
theorem posterity_does_not_reach_the_fit : Satisfiable (posterityCase.premises
    ++ protoevangeliumAsFitting.premises)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="idiom_does_not_reach_the_fit"></a>
**`idiom_does_not_reach_the_fit`**

**Nor does Lewis.** The idiom of Hagar and Rebekah bears on what the wording
signifies, not on what it fits once fulfilled.

```lean
theorem idiom_does_not_reach_the_fit : Satisfiable (idiomCase.premises ++
    protoevangeliumAsFitting.premises)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="whereTheSignifyingReadingMeetsLeupold"></a>
**`whereTheSignifyingReadingMeetsLeupold`**

**Why Leupold stands against the hinge, read as Luther reads it.** The crux
is Leupold's step: "her seed" is first collective, the woman's posterity, and
the woman is named because she was deceived, so the wording does not itself signify
a birth without a human father. No one can hold both Leupold's case and the
hinge read Luther's way; which gives way is the dispute's question, and
`Dispute.Genesis` finds a tie. What cannot be held with Leupold is the hinge
together with the reading, nothing else in the strand, and the step is rated
`disputed`: Irenaeus grants both its grounds, and Henry the second, and both
read the verse of the Virgin's son.

**Why *Leupold on 'her seed': her posterity, named for the deception* stands against *Protoevangelium strand (Genesis 3:15), read as what the wording itself signifies*.**

- **The crux:** \\((P_{50} \land P_{56} \land P_{57}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{54}\\), a premise of *Leupold on 'her seed': her posterity, named for the deception*.
- **What it does:** its conclusion does not follow without it.
- **Granted:** \\(P_{50}\\), \\(P_{56}\\), \\(P_{57}\\), which the break also needs.
- **Where the rival breaks:** \\(P_{53}\\), \\(P_{53} \rightarrow P_{54}\\) cannot be held together with \\((P_{50} \land P_{56} \land P_{57}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{54}\\) and \\(P_{50}\\), \\(P_{56}\\), \\(P_{57}\\); each is needed for the break, and without the crux they stand.
- **What this rests on:**
  - \\(P_{50}\\) Genesis 3:15 says that 'her seed' will strike the serpent's head — *consensus*: Gen 3:15; [`bhs-1997`](../bibliography.md#bhs-1997), app. Gen 3:15

<a id="whereTheSignifyingReadingMeetsLewis"></a>
**`whereTheSignifyingReadingMeetsLewis`**

**Why Lewis stands against the hinge, read as Luther reads it.** The crux is
Lewis's step: Genesis speaks of Hagar's and Rebekah's seed too, so the woman's
seed at 3:15 does not by itself signify a birth without a human father. Rated
`disputed`, on Jimmy Akin, who grants that a woman's seed "is not outside the
bounds of Hebrew expression" and agrees with the "many" who have "rightly seen"
the wording as "a hint of the Virgin Birth".

**Why *Lewis on 'her seed': Genesis says it of Hagar and Rebekah too* stands against *Protoevangelium strand (Genesis 3:15), read as what the wording itself signifies*.**

- **The crux:** \\((P_{50} \land P_{58}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{54}\\), a premise of *Lewis on 'her seed': Genesis says it of Hagar and Rebekah too*.
- **What it does:** its conclusion does not follow without it.
- **Granted:** \\(P_{50}\\), \\(P_{58}\\), which the break also needs.
- **Where the rival breaks:** \\(P_{53}\\), \\(P_{53} \rightarrow P_{54}\\) cannot be held together with \\((P_{50} \land P_{58}) \rightarrow \lnot P_{54}\\) and \\(P_{50}\\), \\(P_{58}\\); each is needed for the break, and without the crux they stand.
- **What this rests on:**

  - \\(P_{58}\\) Genesis speaks of a woman's seed in ordinary births: Hagar's and Rebekah's — *consensus*: Gen 16:10; Gen 24:60; [`lewis-womans-seed-1991`](../bibliography.md#lewis-womans-seed-1991), pp. 299–300
  - the step itself — *disputed*: [`lewis-womans-seed-1991`](../bibliography.md#lewis-womans-seed-1991), pp. 299–300; [`lewis-womans-seed-1991`](../bibliography.md#lewis-womans-seed-1991), p. 319; [`akin-woman-seed-serpent-1999`](../bibliography.md#akin-woman-seed-serpent-1999)

<a id="whatHerSeedMarks"></a>
**`whatHerSeedMarks`**

**What the woman's seed marks, read both ways.** The claim is the
protoevangelium strand's hinge: the seed being named as the woman's marks a
birth with no human father. These are the two readings found in the sources;
a reader with a third would add a third horn.

Read as what the wording itself signifies (Luther's reading), it cannot be held
together with Leupold's case or with Lewis's. Each breaks it at a step rated
`disputed`, not at a ground. Leupold's grounds, that the seed is named the
woman's because she was deceived and that "her seed" is first collective, her
posterity, are rated `wellSupported` and `disputed`; Lewis's, that Genesis says "her
seed" of Hagar and of Rebekah, each with a father, is common ground. What is
contested is the step from them to "so the wording does not signify a birth
without a father". A reader who takes those steps rejects Luther's reading. One
who grants the grounds and refuses the steps need not, as Irenaeus does with
Leupold's and Akin with Lewis's. "Cannot be held together" says that no one
can hold both, not which gives way: `Dispute.Genesis` weighs that, and finds a
tie.

Read as what the wording fits, once fulfilled (Leupold's and Keil's reading),
neither case touches it: Leupold and Keil hold it. But the reading rests on the
virginal conception itself (`maryConceivedAsVirgin`). That is rated `disputed`
because Brown, the historian this argument cites, leaves the question
unresolved; the rating records that it is contested, not that the library
doubts it. On this reading the strand can show that the promise suits a birth
already believed, not that the promise foretold it.

Neither reading is a straw man: read either way, the strand's premises can all
be true together.

**Every reading of \\(P_{53}\\), answered.** *Protoevangelium strand (Genesis 3:15)* holds \\(P_{53}\\). It is read 2 ways here, and each reading is checked; none can be left out.
